acts.sum: Three routes lead into the same question, framed through Michael McKenna's distinction between useful and harmful bias. One has you analyze AI text and image outputs for gender or other biases directly. Another sends you into case studies of law enforcement case-management systems, hiring algorithms, or facial recognition, with COMPAS and OASys among the materials. The third is a jigsaw, where each group takes one type of AI bias, works out its implications and how to spot it, and then teaches the class what it found. acts.t: AI, Authorship, and Citation Practices

acts.sum: Two game-like, paper-based use-case ideas carry this, and neither needs a computer. In the first you add probability weightings to a network of word-type nodes until the chain generates grammatical phrases; in the second you build a chain out of an existing text extract, drawing a [Start] box linked to the first word and then, for each 'current word', counting its occurrences and drawing weighted arrows to the words that follow, closing with a [Stop] box after the last word. Running the finished chain generates text probabilistically, and you can see exactly why it produced what it did, because you drew every weight yourself. The discussion afterwards asks what these word-to-word preferences reveal about how language models work and what they imply for linguistics.

srp: Identify benzene substitution patterns from measured infrared spectra while learning coding and model evaluation.

Students work through introductory Python and data-processing notebooks, interpolate and normalize spectra, and inspect the 630–880 cm−1 region with PCA. They evaluate classification using 20 principal components over repeated 67:33 training/test splits, then collect two unknown spectra and classify them with the full-spectrum library.

acts.sum: In this optional third-year chemistry practical, small groups of students learn data processing and machine-learning evaluation by identifying ortho, meta, and para substitution patterns of benzene derivatives from infrared spectra. Working through introductory Python and Jupyter notebooks, students interpolate and normalize a labeled library of spectra, inspect the diagnostic region with principal component analysis, and evaluate a k-nearest-neighbors classifier over repeated training and test splits. They then measure two unknown samples on an ATR infrared spectrometer and classify them against the full-spectrum library. The classifier supplies predicted labels; students judge its performance from held-out results, with demonstrators supporting interpretation. The outcome is a set of predicted assignments, visualized spectral structure, and model-performance results.
acts.t: Classify measured infrared spectra to identify regioisomers in a Python machine-learning practical
acts.tool: Python; Jupyter notebooks; pandas; PCA; k-nearest neighbors; ATR infrared spectrometer

srp: Prioritize relevant titles and abstracts for a human systematic-review screener.

Titles and abstracts from a completed search are imported and initial relevant and irrelevant examples labeled. The reviewer labels the next ranked record, the model retrains, and the cycle repeats; labeled and ranked remaining records are exported at the chosen stopping point.
Human screening decisions and a prioritized remaining record set.

acts.sum: Systematic reviewers use ASReview's active learning to bring the records most likely to be relevant to the top of the screening queue while every inclusion decision stays with a person. The reviewer imports titles and abstracts from a completed search and labels a few prior examples, at least one relevant and one irrelevant; a text classifier ranks the remaining records, the reviewer labels the next-ranked record, and the model retrains as each label arrives. The reviewer sets the inclusion criteria, decides when to stop screening, and exports the labeled and ranked records. The source cautions that stopping rules require care because complete recall is not guaranteed for a new review, and its feature space omits author names and citation networks to avoid authority bias. acts.t: Prioritize systematic-review screening with active learning while humans make every inclusion decision

Following a tutorial built on a published lung atlas, the researcher registers raw counts and batch covariates, fits the scVI variational model, and inspects latent neighbors, clusters, and visualizations; scANVI can optionally be initialized from the same model with supplied cell-type labels. The integration is then benchmarked by comparing biological-conservation metrics with batch-mixing metrics, because stronger batch removal can erase real biological signal, and the researcher decides which integration to keep on that evidence. acts.sum: An analyst who needs to find records referring to the same person or entity across files without a shared unique identifier uses Splink, an open-source probabilistic record-linkage library. The analyst defines blocking rules that limit which pairs are compared and specifies how fields such as names and dates are compared; the software estimates prior and non-match parameters and uses expectation maximization to learn match parameters without labeled training data, then predicts a match probability for each candidate pair. acts.sum: Before retraining a classifier, an analyst uses cleanlab to find training examples whose labels are probably wrong. The analyst generates out-of-sample predicted class probabilities through cross-validation, runs cleanlab's data and label issue detection to rank suspect examples by estimated label quality, and then inspects and corrects the flagged labels or compares a workflow that prunes them. The corrected or pruned data are used to retrain the model, and performance is compared on separately evaluated data. A model's disagreement with a label is a reason to look rather than proof of an annotation error, so the analyst's review of flagged examples against independent evidence is the step that decides. The tutorial uses a small synthetic four-class dataset and can simulate perfect human correction, which a real review does not guarantee.
acts.t: Audit noisy labels using out-of-sample predictions and human review

acts.sum: Researchers in social work and human-computer interaction use anchored topic modeling to examine how risk, protective, systemic, and procedural factors interact across the case histories of families in a family-preservation program. Case notes are arranged chronologically, cleaned, and anonymized; researchers read sample histories and use a socioecological framework to choose anchor words that steer Anchored CorEx toward domain-relevant topics. They fit and compare models, then several authors interpret topics independently before reconciling labels and using axial coding to relate them, and they compare topic patterns across normalized segments of each history. acts.sum: Before using AI images in Bible teaching, you select scenes deeply rooted in Christian iconography; the source used the Baptism of Jesus and the Last Supper. For each, you issue a deliberately vague prompt first, to see which iconographic patterns the image system produces by default, and then a targeted prompt that adds explicit references to Catholic symbolism and states the religious-education purpose. You keep the first image returned for each prompt, with no refinement, and compare the pair for narrative or interpretive character, theological depth, symbolic coherence, and Western cultural stereotyping, and against selected works of sacred art. The teacher must judge whether either image is theologically adequate for teaching and turn the comparison into didactic recommendations. In the source, both tiers showed shallow theology, symbolic oversimplification, and Western stereotypes.

acts.sum: A religion teacher presents an AI-generated image of a biblical scene as material to be examined rather than as an illustration, and introduces the idea of symbolic dispersion: religious elements added without regard to narrative, historical, or cultural context. Students identify the inconsistencies in the image, say how each should be corrected, and place each element accurately within the biblical passage. The student must judge each element against the biblical text and its historical setting. The exercise ends in reflection on how generative AI handles biblical interpretation. The source calls this visual debugging and frames it as turning students from observers into interpreters.

acts.sum: In a community college business ethics course, a discussion assignment in the unit on technology asks students to complete the week's readings and write their own answers to two questions about technology and privacy before any AI use. Each student then chooses a free generative AI chatbot, has it answer the same questions, and cites the chatbot fully. acts.sum: In a first-year veterinary anatomy course taught as a flipped classroom, students prepare with interactive videos and then work in class in groups of about six, with ChatGPT as a virtual group member used only during those sessions. Each group puts a set question to it in Spanish or English, and students are also encouraged to write their own. acts.sum: This participatory workshop for journalism students builds skill in recognizing automated social media accounts in political disinformation. In the first phase the instructor explains political communication online and the manipulation of the electoral public sphere, then gives a pretest in which students judge ten Twitter accounts as automated or not. In the second phase the class sees the pretest results, the instructor formalizes the intuitive knowledge students already showed and teaches the metadata features that mark bots, students try detection tools on the accounts they judged, and they take a comparable self-assessment test with items isolating single profile features in screenshots, plus open comments on how they identified accounts. acts.sum: A program director reviews every module in a degree program against a framework of four AI literacy dimensions: know and understand AI, use and apply AI, evaluate and create with AI, and AI ethics. Each dimension comes with a learning objective, a checklist of teaching use-case ideas, and candidate tools. The director marks where a dimension is developed nowhere in the program, approaches the organizers of modules best placed to carry each missing dimension, and works with them to integrate it rather than imposing it. Where a dimension cannot be fitted into the curriculum, the director arranges workshops, clubs, or special project groups instead. The audit ends with a check that all four dimensions are covered and build progressively, so students are competent in each by graduation. The director must judge which modules can credibly carry which dimension.
acts.t: Audit a degree program against four AI literacy dimensions, find the gaps, and close them module by module or extracurricularly

acts.sum: A module organizer decides which of four AI literacy dimensions the module should develop, rather than attempting all four, and reads each chosen dimension's learning objective. You then work down that dimension's checklist of teaching use-case ideas, ticking those that fit the module's content and level, and choose tools from its candidate list. Use-case ideas range from formulating queries and comparing responses, AI-assisted note-taking with later reflection, and summarizing readings, through literature and systematic review support and data analysis, to evaluating a dataset and reporting the strengths and weaknesses of both data and tool. Where students will rely on AI output, the framework pairs the use-case idea with in-class reflection and critical evaluation. If ethics is in scope, you set the module's AI assessment policy and acknowledgment rules and teach limitations such as paywalled sources and non-existent references.

acts.sum: The Co-Creative Mentoring Model pairs educators as mentors and mentees and works through four phases. In Preparation, facilitators scaffold readiness for gender-responsive, AI-enhanced teaching. In Co-Creation, each pair uses ChatGPT to generate lesson prompts, assessments, and simplified content and Canva to create accessible visuals, receives feedback, and produces open educational resources that are evaluated for inclusivity and freedom from bias. acts.sum: In a distance-learning Java programming course, the course coordinator builds a practice application in which GPT-4, reached through an API, returns immediate feedback on students' code. Rather than accepting open-ended work, the application offers predefined tasks mapped to the same skill taxonomy and criteria as the graded assignment, and evaluates each submission for correctness, coding style, efficiency, and adherence to good practice, pitching explanations to the learner's level: foundational explanations and error analysis for beginners, optimization suggestions for more advanced learners. Students use it during self-managed study before attempting the graded assignment and may resubmit as often as they wish without penalty, refining their code each time. The pilot at Open University Malaysia involved 24 volunteers in a Diploma in Information Technology course, evaluated through a focus group.

acts.sum: Before putting generative AI output into an openly licensed resource, a faculty author runs a due-diligence check for infringement of individual protected works. The first step is to read the prompt critically: a prompt aimed at a trademarked character invites infringement, while prompts for an abstract book cover with a beach and a whale or a three-paragraph description of hydrocarbons are unlikely to. For text output, the author searches the web to make sure the exact language does not already exist in copyrighted content; for images, they run a reverse image search with a tool such as TinEye or Google Images. Output with no identical match is treated as likely includable; output that matches a protected work is not used. The guidance notes that US copyright does not protect styles or ideas and points to fair-use codes for OER.

acts.sum: Before any student meets a nursing chatbot simulation, faculty evaluate the prompt that configures it. The first phase of the AIMS framework scores the prompt on six instructional domains using a 0-2 rubric: clinical and content credibility; alignment with the educational objectives and intended cognitive level; persona clarity, meaning whether the bot's role and tone are defined; inclusivity and cultural competence of the scenario and language; transparency about the AI's identity to learners; and personalization to learner needs. Domains that score low point to revisions in the prompt before deployment and before Phase 2, which evaluates the chatbot in live interaction. The authors state that prompt design is where inaccurate, biased, or unsafe interactions can be prevented, and they also demonstrated automating the scoring with a GPT-4.0-based Eval-Bot v1.
acts.t: Pre-deployment review of an AI simulation prompt against six instructional domains (AIMS Phase 1)

acts.sum: An instructor and a teaching assistant build a classroom card game on international trade and population health for fifteen sovereign states. They use ChatGPT to compile historical health-affecting events, build economic profiles with GDP, per-capita indicators, and import-export portfolios, decide which resources each state starts with and must obtain, and run repeated simulations to check that the allocations could realistically be met through trade. acts.sum: In a 75-minute undergraduate public health class, groups of two or three represent sovereign states, dividing the roles of Trade Representative, Health Minister, and Finance Minister. Each group holds three to ten resource cards according to its nation's GDP and must meet its health needs through trade. Three ten-minute rounds stand for 2018, 2019, and 2020; trading starts among designated partners and opens more widely at the end of each round, and the 2020 round simulates the COVID-19 pandemic with heavy restrictions. The instructor plays the US Trade Representative and the teaching assistant plays US aid agencies, introducing event cards and observing against the learning objectives. Reflection runs between rounds, by regional bloc, and as a class debrief, followed by a written reflection within 48 hours. Students are told the background data and graphics were AI-assisted.

acts.sum: To produce neurological occupational therapy case studies for teaching, the authors prompt ChatGPT (3.5) and judge the results, finding the first cases thin on background. They refine the prompt through four versions, building in the Occupational Therapy Intervention Process Model and adding temporal, environmental, social, motivational, and functional context. The final prompt requires three parts per case: a scenario with demographics and background, OT assessment results with subjective and objective data, and clinical questions on treatment goals and considerations for implementation. Five cases (four stroke, one spinal cord injury) are generated in one session to keep presentation uniform. Ten experienced OT professors and clinicians then rate each case for clinical realism, information comprehensiveness, and educational value on a five-point scale. The source states that the cases' effect on student learning was not tested.

acts.sum: Researchers select published occupational therapy case reports against explicit inclusion criteria, remove personal information from each case introduction and initial evaluation, and enter each case into GPT-4 from a newly created account with one fixed zero-shot prompt asking for a program in table form with training name, content, duration, frequency, and load. The published intervention and the generated program are put into the same five-field format. Experienced therapists from different specialties then score agreement between them from 4 (complete) to 0 (complete disagreement) and comment on the points of comparison. The model's output is the object being measured; the therapists' judgment of clinical specificity and individualization is the reference. In the source, every generated program scored 2 or lower, with reviewers describing the content as general and insufficiently specialized.

acts.sum: This Programming Historian lesson builds a Naive Bayes classifier over the Old Bailey Online archive of London criminal trials from 1674 to 1913. Because every trial is annotated in XML with offense, verdict, and witness details, the archive supplies a human standard: you download the trials, create cross-validation samples, train and test the classifier, and check its category assignments against the curators' annotation, then extract the features most indicative of each category. acts.sum: A health sciences librarian turns an incoming information request into a prompt the way a PICO question is built from a clinical scenario. You fill six slots: Task (what is to be identified), Context (population, condition, or scope), Example (the kind of instance to focus on), Persona (who the output is for and why), Format (for instance a detailed paragraph with subheadings), and Tone (for instance professional and thorough). acts.sum: Students learn a four-stage procedure for checking whether a claim in a text is actually warranted by the source it cites. In consolidation they confirm that each in-text citation matches a bibliography entry, that every entry is cited, that the item matches a record that does or did exist, and that the record is retrievable. In textual entailment they look in the cited work for content that supports or contradicts the claim. In validity they judge whether that content is empirically warranted in its own study, and in transferability whether it carries over to the citing context. srp: As the source frames it, to have students translate theoretical research into executable analytical instructions, treating system instructions, schemas, and iteration logs as scholarly artifacts.

Four phases with checkpoints: framework memo and annotated bibliography; an operational blueprint of primitives with self-assessment; system instructions with test-run documentation and a versioned prompt journal logging failures; deployment in an API playground or no-code tool tested across multiple texts with documentation of what it highlights and obscures.

acts.sum: Across a fifteen-week module in a prototype undergraduate syllabus, students translate a critical theoretical framework into executable instructions for a language model. They first write a framework selection memo and an annotated bibliography, then decompose the theory into operational primitives, each with action verbs, the textual evidence it maps to, and edge cases, and reflect on which concepts were hardest to operationalize. Next they write system instructions with a persona, contextual grounding, the primitives as explicit instructions, negative constraints, and a required output structure, test them on a sample text, and keep a prompt journal logging every version and its rationale, including failed prompts and why they failed. Finally they deploy the instrument in an API playground or no-code tool, test it across several texts, and document what it highlights and what it obscures.
acts.t: Operationalizing a critical theory as system instructions and a data schema, with a logged iteration history as the assessed artifact

srp: Have learners practice critical analysis of AI content and the tool that produced it.

acts.sum: After establishing that AI content can look accurate and appropriate without being so, the instructor models a critical analysis and sets it as a learning use-case idea. Students apply four considerations: content accuracy checked against trusted resources, bias awareness, ethical considerations, and source verification. They then work through two question banks. About the tool: who created and trained it, on what dataset, under what privacy policy, with what limitations, and who is harmed or benefits. About the text: what is present and missing, word choices, audience, reliability, sources, and biases. Students close by searching the internet for the original sources the tool may have drawn on. The output is a written analysis of the tool and its text.

Under tool effectiveness they characterize how accurate, precise, and contextualized the responses were and whether the tool hallucinated. Under critical evaluation they describe how they decided which responses to trust, when the tool seemed most reliable, and whether prior knowledge of the topic is needed to use it. Under usage they identify which prompts produced the best and worst responses, when the tool got caught in a loop, and what they would recommend to next year's students. acts.sum: An instructional designer with learning objectives already fixed uses an AI assistant to draft weekly lesson plans from chapters of an open textbook, here for a four-week faculty learning circle on HyFlex teaching that is itself taught in HyFlex. Because the assistant could not open the book from a link, three chapters were downloaded and attached as PDFs along with a description of the objectives, audience, and delivery format. acts.sum: Before a remote chemistry laboratory runs, instructors configure the AI assistant students will be able to consult. Through the platform's configuration interface they enter information about the laboratory setup, instruments, and safety guidelines, add excerpts from their own laboratory manual as the assistant's context, and write behavioral constraints, most notably that the assistant must not give complete numerical solutions. The assistant, built on GPT-4o, has no internet access and answers only text questions related to the experiment. Once deployed alongside the experiment, its interactions with students are logged by the platform for later analysis. The instructor's judgment lies in what context to supply and what the assistant must refuse to do, so that it supports reasoning without doing the calculations students are meant to perform.

acts.sum: An environmental data science course for upper-level undergraduate and graduate students balances AI-assisted work against assessment that shows what students can do without it, through four components. In the first nine lessons students learn Python basics through two assignments completed without AI assistance. Formal guidance on AI tools, prompting, and responsible use follows mid-course, and from lesson ten students complete project-based assignments and a term project on datasets of their own interest with AI coding assistance, documenting their AI use. A 75-minute paper-based in-class exam tests conceptual understanding with AI prohibited. Multi-step case studies, such as the effect of COVID-19 on air quality, let AI help with processing while students connect the steps and interpret the results themselves. acts.sum: In an environmental data science course, students work multi-step case studies on real datasets, such as the effect of COVID-19 on air quality in South Florida or changes in rainfall under different CMIP6 future scenarios for North and South Florida. AI coding assistants and chatbots may carry out mechanical steps such as data cleaning, processing, and analysis, but students decide how to connect the steps into a solution path, interpret the results, and draw the conclusions themselves, synthesizing a cohesive solution. The authors design it this way because AI tools can shift the cognitive work from solving a problem to merely validating generated answers. Two homework case studies were implemented; the authors also recommend a take-home exam in the same form, which the source presents as a future addition rather than something already run.

acts.sum: In a third-year architectural design studio, students move from describing design concepts to a large language model to controlling image generation themselves. They generate and refine preliminary images through iterative text-to-image and image-to-image prompting, train LoRA models on discipline-specific reference libraries, and assemble ComfyUI node workflows (ControlNet, inpainting, mask-based drawing, high-resolution fix) to test design variations and manage visual style, comparing base models for the project. acts.sum: Before addressing the AI at all, the student writes an initial design intention for a pavilion in a fortress setting. They then send a provocative prompt, asking the model to ignore the historical context and defend that choice, to reconcile being fully open and fully closed, or to argue as an architect who dislikes the site, and receive three variants, one of them deliberately problematic. The student writes a theory-based analysis of what the AI got right and wrong, redefines the problem, and runs a second round of prompting and analysis. The work ends with a final concept as collage or sketch and a reflective report of at least 500 words, submitted in one PDF with the intention, both dialogue rounds, and the analyses. Mentors supply the prompt techniques and review the process documentation.

In class they first derive the least-squares formulation themselves, then spend 45 minutes conveying the problem to the chatbot step by step, breaking the equations into parts, to generate MATLAB code. acts.sum: Statistics faculty test how chatbots perform on the validated final-exam question bank of an undergraduate statistics course for engineering students. They first check the items for missing special characters, formulas, or tables, confirm the chatbot understands the questions, and then present 52 questions, 156 items in all, to ChatGPT 3.5 three times each in randomized order. Every answer is compared with the expert professors' answers, and each error is categorized by statistical field and sub-field, question type, reason, and reasoning complexity. In a second, qualitative stage the 36 questions with errors are taken into semi-structured interviews with chatbots using a grounded-theory approach, including confrontations in which one chatbot's answer is put to another and agreement, disagreement, and revision are analyzed. The result is an error profile and categories of chatbot behavior under challenge.

acts.sum: Outside its project phase, an undergraduate engineering probability and statistics course has students work basic probability, combinatorics, and Gaussian interval problems by hand or with a calculator, without notes, and learn thumb rules for one- and two-standard-deviation intervals. The stated purpose is confidence in the principles and a simple reference against which to check whether a computational tool is being used correctly. The authors tie this to generative AI: because AI can now write the code for such tools, checking tool usage against a hand-worked answer matters more. Their example is MATLAB's erf() function, whose two-sided definition requires scaling inputs by one over the square root of two before Z-score use. Later in the term the course shifts to team machine-learning projects in Python on real datasets.
acts.t: Hand-worked solutions as the check on tool and AI-written code in engineering statistics

Each question is assigned a Bloom's level with the Blooming Biology Tool. Student responses are sampled at random from a cohort that finished before ChatGPT's release, so none could have used it. GPT-4o answers every item, ten times for each multiple-choice question, and free responses are generated and then rewritten in paragraph form so their style matches student writing. Three graders score all responses blind against a standardized rubric, and performance is compared by Bloom's level to locate the items most exposed to the tool. Student answers are graded alongside the model's, not given to it. In the source, students outperformed the model overall, which was weakest at the remember and apply levels.

For a poorly annotated four-lane DNA footprinting gel, students identify the technique, describe its key steps, and interpret each lane as a condition or control; other items pair an image with multiple-choice options so a vague answer is not possible. The instructors test the new items against GPT-4o, including a version without the image, to see how much the image carries the question. They also revise rubrics so graders have the ideal answer, only the first experiment a student proposes is graded, and the choice of technique must be justified, and they weight take-home work toward applying known procedures in new situations. acts.sum: In a third-year hydraulic engineering course, student pairs run the direct shear test in soil mechanics after common instruction on shear-strength theory and the apparatus. Within a mandatory online Ethics of Research course, students complete an approximately five-hour AI ethics module, choose from seven real-world case studies, reflect explicitly on ethical considerations and potential solutions, and complete pre- and post-intervention knowledge, awareness, and open-response measures.
Written ethical analyses and reflections on a chosen case, plus pre- and post-module responses.
acts.sum: Inside a mandatory online research-ethics course that graduate science and engineering students take before submitting a research proposal, a module of about five hours addresses the ethics of AI. Students choose among seven real-world case studies of ethical dilemmas in AI development and use, such as autonomous vehicles, misuse of personal data from a dating website, and AI-generated art imitating well-known artists. For the chosen case they analyze the dilemma, reflect explicitly on the ethical considerations involved and propose possible solutions, drawing on international guidance including the OECD Recommendation on AI and IEEE reports. No AI tool is used; AI systems and their documented uses are the subject matter. The study measured knowledge, perceived awareness, and open responses to a photograph prompt before and after the module.
acts.t: Case-based, explicit-reflective AI ethics module for graduate science and engineering students

They then upload each source to NotebookLM for a summary or analysis and assess what comes back for accuracy against the source, relevance, and depth, noting missing nuance or evidence. Using their notes and that evaluation, they write 150-200-word annotations in their own words in APA 7 or their discipline's style, adding their own judgment of each source's reliability and contribution, and check that no generated text was copied. A closing acknowledgment of up to 200 words describes their verification steps, what the AI missed, and whether it hallucinated. Faculty are advised to test the tool on academic sources first.

acts.sum: Students write a short in-class essay on a topic they already know, using only human-generated sources and distraction-free tools. They then prompt a chatbot on the same topic to brainstorm research questions, simplify texts, map a research plan, or suggest sources, documenting each step and how it affected their thinking. They evaluate their essay twice, once with a rubric co-created with the chatbot and once with personal or peer criteria, weighing the AI rubric's limits. A Socratic dialogue follows in which they press the chatbot with 'why', 'how', and 'what if' through three to five layers. They have the chatbot revise the original essay, write another human-only draft, ask a classmate and the chatbot to compare versions for rhetoric and voice, produce a final revision in their own voice, and answer reflection questions on authorship.
acts.t: Alternating AI-free and AI-assisted essay drafting, with Socratic interrogation of the chatbot

acts.sum: A writer takes a draft to a chatbot for feedback rather than for rewriting. They paste in a feedback prompt developed on the Peer & AI Review + Reflection (PAIRR) project, which asks the chatbot to describe two strengths and two possible areas for revision with quotations from the draft, and add the draft and, optionally, the assignment instructions and rubric. They then treat the first response as the start of a conversation: pushing back on comments that seem wrong, asking for clarification, requesting a different version of the feedback, raising what it did not address, exploring what they are unsure about, and asking for writing strategies. The writer decides which comments to act on and revises the draft themselves, then steps back and takes the draft to a human reader, since the source states chatbot feedback does not replace peer review or tutoring.

srp: To assess learning during the stages of a process rather than only from finished work, letting AI assist specific thinking steps without displacing students' own idea generation.

Segment a large project into components with feedback and revision, weight grading toward process, and have students free-write first, then use AI chatbots to explore areas for investigation based on their own ideas, then critique and revise the AI-generated ideas into an outline.

acts.sum: Within a large project broken into smaller components with repeated chances for feedback and revision, and with grading weighted toward process rather than the finished work, students begin with low-stakes free-writing such as brainstorming, without AI. They then use a chatbot to explore possible areas for further investigation based on the ideas their own exploratory writing produced, rather than asking it to generate ideas from nothing. Finally they critique the AI-suggested areas and revise them into an outline. The guide places this among thinking steps, such as brainstorming, formulating a position, or outlining a solution, where allowing AI might help students' process, and says instructors may assess learning better at these stages than from finished work.

srp: To design a high-accuracy workflow that reduces reviewer workload by using a large language model to screen titles and abstracts, and to develop optimal prompts for that review.

Human-screened records are split into development batches and a reserved test set; each PICO and exclusion criterion is written as a Boolean prompt field; prompts are refined on 50-record sets until all relevant records are found; final prompts are run on the test set and on two later review updates, and performance statistics are calculated.
A validated prompt set with base, modified, and final wording, plus sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and workload-reduction statistics.
Comparison with human screening decisions on held-out test and validation sets; short or missing abstracts flagged for manual review.
acts.sum: A systematic-review team builds and validates prompts so that GPT-4o can screen titles and abstracts for a living review. Human screening decisions already made for the review serve as the reference standard. Records are split into a development set, drawn in batches, and a reserved test set, and two later review updates are held back for validation. Each PICO eligibility element and each exclusion criterion becomes a Boolean prompt field that the model answers TRUE or FALSE, with exclusion criteria tested first. Prompts are refined fifty records at a time until every relevant record is identified or further changes stop helping. The final prompts are then run on the test set and the validation updates, and sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and workload reduction are calculated. Very short or missing abstracts are flagged for manual review.
acts.t: Iterative PICO-derived prompt development for LLM title/abstract screening, with held-out test and validation sets
acts.tool: GPT-4o; EPPI Reviewer; OpenAI API via Azure

srp: To understand whether variability in model outputs affects screening accuracy, and to what extent, before relying on the prompts in future review updates.

The team selects 50 random records, submits the final prompts for that same set ten times, counts agreements with human screeners and divides by the number of runs, and interprets the percentage against published bands, reporting overall and per-criterion consistency.
A consistency percentage for the overall decision and individual exclusion criteria, and a judgment on whether stability is adequate.
Agreement with human screeners across repeated runs, interpreted against published accuracy bands.
acts.sum: Because a language model can give different answers to the same input, a systematic-review team checks how stable its final screening prompts are before relying on them in later updates. Fifty records are selected at random and submitted to the final prompts ten times. For each run the team counts how often the model's decision agrees with the human screeners and divides agreements by the number of runs to get a consistency percentage, reported separately for the overall include-or-exclude decision and for each exclusion criterion. The percentage is read against published bands, with 80 to 95 percent treated as on par with human reviewers, 60 to 80 percent as near par, and below 60 percent as subpar. The team then judges whether stability is adequate for the review and for which criteria it is not.
acts.t: Reliability audit of AI screening prompts by repeated runs on the same records

acts.sum: Before using a generative AI tool on research data, a researcher classifies the data as public, protected, or highly protected and reads a permission matrix that crosses those classes with three deployment types: locally run models, enterprise models, and public models. Public data may go to all three; protected data only to local or enterprise models; highly protected data is conditional on a local model and not permitted elsewhere. The researcher then checks the governing policies, namely their own institution's endorsed-tools list, the research funder's rules (including a prohibition on reviewers putting grant applications into AI systems) and the target journal's AI policy, and weighs the trade-off between control at the local end and performance at the public end. No AI tool is used in making the decision; the output is a policy-traceable choice of tool class for a given dataset or task.
acts.t: Data-sensitivity by model-type matrix for deciding which AI tool a research task may use

srp: Make AI use in a research group transparent and reconstructable, so problems are caught with the mentor's support before submission and AI use can be reported accurately in publications.

acts.sum: Anyone in the lab who uses generative AI for research or research-adjacent work tells their mentor within one week of use, or one week before external submission if that is sooner, and tells collaborators inside and outside the lab before or during the work rather than afterward. acts.sum: Before adopting an AI tool that evaluates data management plans, data management experts at two university libraries run a validation. They evaluate a set of plans with the tool (28 in the source, producing 556 expert labels at about 50 minutes per plan), record their own labels against its judgments, and sort the criteria questions into five complexity categories, from explicit check to adequacy judgment. acts.sum: Participants use a four-level reflective frame to examine how they use generative AI rather than whether they use it. For each of ten human purposes (explore, understand, evaluate, create, plan, rehearse, regulate, curate, reflect, connect) they name the concrete use-case ideas they hand to AI, identify the human capabilities in play that the use could strengthen or erode, and answer a reflective question about their own practice, such as whether they still decide what is worth pursuing when AI generates possibilities. At approval they apply explicit equity criteria, asking for evidence of representative training data and of the vendor's awareness of system limitations, and defer approval where transparency or reliability cannot be shown until identified risks are mitigated. For each proposed system they carry out an environmental impact assessment, ask the vendor to disclose energy use and sustainability measures, prefer efficient, lower-energy models where educational outcomes are comparable, and write energy sourcing and carbon commitments into procurement documentation. Groups next draft a sample class contract, a set of norms for a setting that permits some AI use, and may use generative AI tools in doing so while considering the implications of that use. Prompting questions ask how existing class norms extend to AI, when AI use could disrupt trust between teachers and students, when it could support or undermine learning, and when and how students should acknowledge it. acts.sum: Graduate students from a design course take part in a series of student-led workshops, facilitated by two peers with no evaluative role and without faculty present. They reflect on their own recent AI use, including uses that fell into gray areas or broke a course policy, compare experiences in pairs and bring key themes to a group discussion informed by a campus committee's survey findings on student and faculty AI use. Each participant then chooses several policy topics from a seeded list, which participants may add to, and uses a worksheet to name a core tension, describe a relevant learning outcome or classroom scenario, and draft a concise conditional policy statement. The research team consolidates the drafts into a smaller set of recommendations, checking them with participants and against the literature, and each participant then visualizes two of them as zine pages, one digital and one on paper, after an introduction to zine making from a visual arts professor. The finished zine circulated across campus and was archived by the university library.
acts.t: Student-led drafting of course AI policy recommendations from accounts of AI use, published as a zine

acts.sum: Student teams in an undergraduate UX design course complete a design project, in the reported case a fitness-tracking experience, with explicit permission to use generative AI tools, including language models, anywhere in their design process. The project brief asks teams to justify each use, credit each AI tool with a citation and an explanation of how they used it, and include a group reflection of 300 to 500 words on the advantages and challenges they met. AI use is optional, and the brief states that neither AI use nor the content of the reflection will lower the project score; the course's usual AI policy is suspended for this project. Teams submit full documentation covering research findings, design process, the reflection, and final artifacts, often with appendices of prompts or conversation logs. From the variation they found across teams, from full citations to vague mentions to none, the authors propose AI contribution statements and documentation recording when in the process AI was used, what content it produced, how it was engaged, and why its output was used, adapted, or discarded.

acts.sum: Museum staff, a faculty member, and a group of undergraduates built a customized language-model interface for a university art museum by scraping the publicly available text metadata for about fourteen thousand objects from its online collection and connecting it to the model through an embeddings service. The curatorial team then prompted the model to propose an exhibition theme, select a checklist of objects for a small gallery, write the introductory text and wall labels, and suggest how the works should be grouped and sequenced, recording the prompting sessions. The resulting exhibition of twenty-one works was installed with annotations beneath the model's labels that point out where it retitled objects, mislabeled media, or attached unrelated information, and that connect those errors to gaps in the metadata and to how the model works. The students' part centered on building the data pipeline and on the ethical questions it raised, including using only public data and limiting what was fed to the model. The reviewer credits this student involvement as the project's most successful element and calls for future versions to document more openly the human decisions behind platform and data choices.

acts.sum: Third-year English majors in a language technologies and digital communication course work in groups of three or four to plan, script, and produce a short educational podcast in English for other learners of English as a foreign language. The course introduces generative tools for text, images, music, and audio editing, and students use them where they choose, mainly for brainstorming ideas, drafting and editing scripts, and making thumbnails and promotional images, with some adding generated music or sound effects. Students receive guidance on attribution, critical evaluation of AI-generated content, and human oversight, and they keep a project log recording the prompts they used and how they integrated or modified the output. In an open-ended questionnaire afterward, students described AI as a helpful collaborator for ideas and language quality but reported generic suggestions and thin local cultural knowledge, as when a request for folklore examples returned Western fairy tales instead of Indonesian ones, which they had to supply themselves. The authors read the study as showing both benefits and a continuing need for human input and oversight.

Each student then hand-writes a half-page proposal for an original scene inspired by the excerpt, using the analyzed variables. Only after that do students expand the proposal into a short slide presentation of the equipment they would use and the images they want to create, drawing on any available text or image generation tools. On submission day the class discusses whether the tools helped; the authors report that students found text tools useful but judged the free image tools of mid-2024 an obstacle, producing images they called “too polished” or “overly hegemonic,” and all said they would have finished faster without AI. Working in a shared spreadsheet, the team first codes a small set of plans together, labeling each lesson task with the highest revised Bloom's Taxonomy level it reaches, using their own pedagogical judgment rather than the verb the chatbot chose, and rating any multicultural content on Banks' four levels of integration. Two members then code the full corpus while two others double-check, resolving discrepancies by consensus. In their corpus of 310 plans and 2,230 lesson tasks, the authors found nearly half of lesson tasks at the remember level and little multicultural content beyond the contributions and additive levels, and they urge teachers to revise rather than adopt AI plans as written.
acts.t: Audit AI-generated lesson plans lesson task by lesson task with Bloom's Taxonomy and Banks' levels

acts.sum: Students in a communications or media course play a classroom version of Turing's imitation game in groups of three to six. One student is the guesser, one is a mediator at a shared screen, and one answers as the human from another room, while a chatbot that the instructor has secretly given a persona (neutral, friendly, devious, or apathetic, with an age and profile) answers the same questions; the mediator retypes both answers into a neutral document so formatting gives neither away. After a stretch of free questioning the identities are revealed, and each group examines the exchange for the cues that separated person from machine, such as verbosity, strained slang, over-precise answers, and tone. A whole-class discussion then moves from whether the machine can pass to how prompting, cultural norms, and the tacit conventions of peer talk shape what counts as intelligent, natural, or 'cringe' speech, drawing on prior readings on the Turing Test and critical AI studies. The author reports that guessers usually spot the machine quickly and that the analysis of why is where the learning happens. The products are each group's account of the linguistic tells it found and a class discussion of how the personae were built.
acts.t: Run a mediated Turing Test with persona-prompted chatbots and analyze the cues that mark machine speech

acts.sum: Teams of four to five students in an organizational communication, management, or leadership course pick a real or hypothetical workplace communication challenge, such as onboarding messages, advice on conflict with a supervisor, or intercultural email. Each team frames the challenge with an organizational communication theory, such as anticipatory socialization, leader–member exchange, or transactive memory, and uses it to define the tool's purpose, inputs, outputs, tone, and constraints. Working in a custom-assistant builder, teams draft and test prompts in class and between the two sessions, logging outputs, inaccuracies, and signs of bias as they iterate. Alongside the prototype they write a documentation guide covering the theory link, configuration and prompts, ethical questions such as bias, privacy, and which tasks still need a person, known limitations, and upkeep. The unit closes with a pitch to the class, where peers and the instructor ask how the tool would fit real workflows and who would maintain it, followed by a discussion of where human communication cannot be replaced. The products are a working prototype and its documentation guide.
acts.t: Design, test, and document a theory-grounded custom AI assistant for a workplace communication task

acts.sum: Preservice language teachers, or in-service teachers building their practice, work through a three-session sequence on feedback literacy. After an introduction to the features of a feedback message (amount, focus, tone, whether to correct errors or only indicate them, and how to phrase comments), each participant writes their own feedback on an authentic sample learner text and records the reasoning behind their choices on a worksheet. Small groups compare that feedback, and the instructor then demonstrates how a chatbot's feedback on a text shifts with differently worded prompts. Between sessions, participants, individually or in groups, prompt a chatbot for feedback on the same learner text, try several prompts, and analyze the output on a second worksheet. In the final session small groups, then the whole class, compare teacher and AI feedback, weighing the strengths and drawbacks of each, the effect of prompts, and whether and how the two might be combined. The products are each participant's own feedback, an analysis of the AI feedback, and a reasoned position on when to use either.
acts.t: Write feedback on a learner text first, then generate AI feedback on the same text and compare the two

acts.sum: Preservice and in-service special educators and related-service providers each write IEP goals for two written student scenarios that give a student's age, grade, disability identification, likes and dislikes, and assessment scores. For one scenario they write the goal unaided; for the other they fill in a structured template (student name, age, primary disability, goal area, present level, condition, behavior, criterion, and time frame), paste it with a one-line instruction into a free chatbot, and copy the generated goal back, with the order of the two conditions randomized. Participants then rate each goal on six items of the Revised IEP/IFSP Goals and Objectives Rating Instrument, which ask whether the target behavior is observable, measurable, functional, generalizable, and teachable across daily tasks and team members. The research team scored the goals with R-GORI, and ChatGPT also scored them against SMART criteria. Expert R-GORI ratings tended to be lower than participant and chatbot ratings; the authors note that formulaic goals can earn rubric points that expert judgment would withhold. Participants also wrote how they would use such tools, and many stressed review, individualization, and privacy. The products are two goals per participant with their rubric self-ratings and a short written reflection.

Students define the task and record AI use; check key drug claims against a claim-specific source hierarchy; rebuild the pharmacological mechanism; test the answer against patient variables; and revise with feedback and a justification note.
A recorded prompt and retained output, checked claims with sources, a mechanism chain, and a revised answer with a correction note.
Each safety- or reasoning-relevant claim is matched to a designated source; unresolved discrepancies go to teacher discussion.
acts.sum: In a formative pharmacology task where AI use is allowed, undergraduate students put a case question to a chatbot before class, for example whether a beta-blocker suits an adult with asthma and newly diagnosed, uncomplicated hypertension. They record the tool, the prompt, and the part of the answer they kept, then pick out the drug claims that matter for safety and check each against a small teacher-provided source set matched to the type of claim: course materials for mechanisms, official labels for product safety, and guidelines for treatment choices. Students rebuild the mechanism as a causal chain from drug target to effect, risk, and monitoring, and test the answer against the patient's details, such as asthma history and the absence of a separate cardiovascular indication. They then revise the answer and write a short correction note stating what changed, why, and which source or case detail justified it. In the authors' worked example, a fluent answer that treats receptor selectivity as nearly absolute is revised to a guideline-based first-line choice. The products are the AI-use record, the source checks, the mechanism chain, and the revised answer with its note.
acts.t: Check an AI answer to a pharmacology case against set sources, rebuild the mechanism, and revise with a note
acts.tool: Any LLM chat interface (the authors mention ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Copilot)

Once a draft exists, they ask a chatbot for feedback one section at a time, using prompts tailored to the task, such as how to restructure the Specific Aims, whether a closing paragraph fits the funder's mission, or how well the text addresses a named review criterion. They treat any suggested wording as inspiration rather than text to paste, fact-check every claim and reference, and use a document-comparison feature to see exactly what changed between their version and an AI-edited one. acts.sum: Medical students work through two patient cases in which the race coefficient in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) equation changes how kidney function is staged and what care follows, answering anonymous in-session polls and discussing each case with a peer facilitator. A short didactic segment traces the history of the equation and its race-correction factor and distinguishes race, ancestry, and genetics. Students then consider what removing race from the equation means for kidney-transplant referral and treatment, including the race-free equation that institutions have since adopted. The algorithm here is a clinical formula rather than a machine-learning system, but the move students practice is the same one needed for AI in health care: following a biased input through to unequal care. The authors report delivering the session four times, virtually and in person, to 55 students across all years of medical school.
acts.t: Trace how a race-corrected clinical algorithm shapes kidney-disease staging and care through case discussion

acts.sum: Midwifery students conduct telehealth visits with generative-AI patient avatars whose detailed social histories, such as rural housing, school and family support, religious practice and dietary needs, surface in conversation only if students ask. Working in pairs, one student takes a full history, forms differential diagnoses, and then offers patient education and a plan of care, while the partner observes, takes notes, can be consulted as a colleague, and gives peer feedback; the pair then swaps roles for a second case. The platform scores each visit against a faculty-written rubric and returns a paragraph of feedback, which is formative only. A faculty-led debrief follows in which students reconstruct their interaction, mark what was correct, omitted, or could improve, compare how the avatar responded to different questions and reflect on their own biases. Working through a sequence of guided questions, they compare raw and normalized frequencies, decide which stop words to filter and why, and note hypotheses suggested by the words that distinguish each document from the rest. They then search keywords in context, sort the concordance lines by position and surrounding words, and draw conclusions about how a term is used, exporting tables and visualizations as evidence. The lesson uses a counting tool rather than a chatbot, so every figure students interpret is computed from the texts themselves.

Small groups then build their own set of three: a real archival photograph with an accurate caption, an AI-generated image with an invented caption, and a real photograph with a misleading caption, drawing real images from trusted archives and using a list of historical-technique terms to prompt the image generator. acts.sum: A workshop for people new to generative AI moves through three phases. In the entry phase, participants share on a common board what they have used a chatbot for and what happened, list pros and cons, and surface their expectations and fears, so the range of uses in the room becomes visible. In the experimentation phase, each participant chooses tools from a provided list to create a written text, an audio piece, an image, and an audiovisual presentation, varying prompts or comparing tools for the same task, and prompts images of a given social group to see what biases appear and how revised prompts change them; participants share what they made. In the exit phase, pairs or small groups analyze their experiments for opportunities and risks for a concrete task, such as whether to use AI for a podcast, with the facilitator asking more critical questions and the group drafting shared practices or house rules. The author, who ran the model with journalism students, journalists, researchers, and communicators, describes it as deliberately starting from personal experience and addressing risks last.

acts.sum: In a business writing course, each major assignment, from a job application to an internal memo, feasibility study, and proposal, goes through a rough draft, an audience analysis, and formal peer review by two or three classmates using assignment-specific criteria. Students then prompt a chatbot for feedback on the same draft, assigning it the role of a supportive peer reviewer and giving it the same checklist or rubric. They write a reflection that compares the peer and chatbot feedback, judges whether each suggestion fits their audience, goals, and writing voice, and sets out a revision plan. After revising, they write a second reflection on how each kind of feedback shaped their changes. Earlier in the course students read and reflect on short readings about AI, and instructors guide them in creating accounts and protecting their data and privacy. The authors report that students valued peers' contextual knowledge, found chatbot feedback actionable but sometimes generic, and in about a quarter of coded reflections in the wider study questioned or corrected the AI feedback.
acts.t: Peer and chatbot feedback on the same professional-genre draft, compared in reflections around revision

acts.sum: A center for teaching and learning runs a funded fellowship in which instructors from any discipline design and carry out classroom studies of whether students' use of generative AI changes their performance on learning outcomes, and for whom. The call for proposals requires a comparison group and supplies options for forming one, asks applicants to name which course assessments will serve as data and whether each is individual or team work, and admits only AI tools that are already built and user-tested. Reviewers score de-identified proposals, reconcile scores in discussion, and hold provisional interviews with promising applicants whose designs have gaps, declining designs that rely on students choosing their own condition. During each study, center staff recommend a delayed transfer task completed without AI so that tool performance is not mistaken for learning, several alternating cycles in within-subjects designs, repeated pilot testing of off-the-shelf tools, a signed written summary of the design, and regular check-ins. Fellows receive stipend installments tied to milestones such as sharing data and submitting a manuscript, along with writing groups, an article template, analysis support, and a panel with journal editors that treats null results as worth publishing.
acts.t: Run a SoTL fellowship on generative AI and learning with proposal rules that keep results interpretable
acts.tool: Off-the-shelf tools such as Copilot and ChatGPT, and instructor-built tools (as named)

acts.sum: A reviewer who has drafted a review for a conference or journal submits the review text and the paper to a multi-model feedback pipeline. Two models independently look for review comments that are vague or generic, questions already answered somewhere in the paper, and unprofessional remarks; an aggregator merges their lists, a critic removes inaccurate or nitpicky items, and a formatter pairs each flagged comment with suggested feedback addressed to the reviewer. Automated reliability tests screen the feedback before it is shown, rejecting items that merely praise the reviewer, address the paper's authors instead, restate the comment, or are malformed. The reviewer reads the suggestions and decides whether to revise; the system neither edits the review nor proposes new critiques. At ICLR 2025 the authors randomized 44,831 reviews, selected 22,467 for feedback, and successfully delivered feedback to 18,946. They report that 26.6% of reviews receiving feedback were updated, and that updated reviews were longer and rated more informative by blinded researchers. The authors publish the prompts and code for running the pipeline on one's own review.
acts.t: Check a draft peer review with an LLM pipeline that flags vague, already-answered, and unprofessional comments
acts.tool: Claude Sonnet 3.5 (June 2024) as backbone at the time of the trial

For the qualitative strand, the researcher avoids asking for cold inductive coding and instead supplies an analytic framework, a theoretical framework, and a few human-coded examples, then compares the chatbot's codes and themes with their own; the author measured agreement with a human coder and found it negligible for cold coding and moderate once examples were given. For the quantitative strand, the researcher shares a codebook, asks for suggested analyses, descriptive tables, and inferential tests, and uses their own statistical judgment to reject suggestions that do not fit the data. Only after both strands are analyzed separately does the researcher combine the findings in one document and ask for a named mixed methods integration, such as a sequential explanatory synthesis or a statistics-by-theme joint display, checking every table against their own version and writing the final interpretation themselves. acts.sum: A team proposing an AI system that will use shared data names a lead and a notetaker and meets to work through a structured template of questions and prompts. The team first records the system's purpose, intended uses, inputs and outputs, and the people it affects, then considers common ethical concerns such as widening inequalities, increased surveillance, changed relationships between stakeholders, environmental effects, and misuse. It sketches best-case and worst-case scenarios, the hurdles and conditions needed for success, and the potential harms, judging each harm's importance, urgency, difficulty, and detectability and noting possible mitigations. A paid panel of patients and members of the public drawn from groups likely to be affected then hears the team present the system and deliberates on the scenarios in a facilitated workshop, possibly surfacing further harms, and the team works these findings back into the template. The completed assessment informs a data-access decision, is published, and is revised when the system changes significantly.

acts.sum: A qualitative researcher carrying out reflexive thematic analysis uses a chatbot in some phases and deliberately sets it aside in others. After replacing names of sites and participants with pseudonyms, the researcher reads the data closely and writes her own familiarization notes, while briefing the chatbot on the research aims, questions, context, and theoretical frameworks. The chatbot proposes deductive and inductive codes and later clusters them into candidate themes and maps; the researcher checks each suggestion against the raw data, corrects miscoded extracts, re-codes material the tool missed, and records every AI-generated code and revision alongside codes and themes left unused. She reviews and develops themes without the chatbot, drawing on participants' social and cultural contexts the tool cannot see, and then uses it only to draft definitions and offer candidate names from which she chooses. The write-up states her positionality, discloses the chatbot's role, and limits later AI use to proofreading.
acts.t: Reflexive thematic analysis with a chatbot in selected phases, pseudonymized data, and a code audit trail

acts.sum: In a first-year writing unit, students examine how recommendation algorithms on the social media platforms they already use personalize what they see. They read about digital literacy, watch a short video series on navigating digital information, and discuss on online boards whether personalization is a form of surveillance and what effective and ethical use would mean. Students then capture screenshots of the news, advertisements, and top posts in their feeds, map which parts of their identity appear in their filter bubble and which are missing, and discuss steps they could take to diversify their feeds, such as changing privacy or location settings. A five-stage sequence: contrasting anecdotes and counterexamples; score distributions set against societal context; confusion matrices with false positive and false negative rates plus a toy model showing base-rate effects and positive predictive value; the vendor's rebuttal and a gender-separated recomputation; and the court's ruling as a route to meaningful human control and automation bias.

acts.sum: In a course on gender knowledge and ethics in AI for computer science and engineering undergraduates, students work through the COMPAS recidivism-risk controversy as a sequence of judgments they are asked to form and then test. They first interpret two contrasting defendant cases from the investigative reporting and are then shown counterexamples drawn from the same public dataset, so that anecdote gives way to statistical questions. Moving through the race-separated score distributions and confusion matrices, the class compares false positive rates, false negative rates, and positive predictive values, and works a two-population toy model in which a system that is fair by design still produces unequal false positive rates when base rates differ. Students then weigh the vendor's rebuttal, recompute predictive value by gender, and discuss the Wisconsin Supreme Court's distinction between a judge considering a score and relying on it, which opens questions of meaningful human control and automation bias. The author describes the aim as deconstructing hasty conclusions so that students hold several fairness metrics and stakeholder positions in view at once.
acts.t: Test quick fairness verdicts on the COMPAS risk tool against error rates, gender, and human control

A registry-curation assistant that can look up and propose but has no function to publish
acts.sum: Curators of a research organization registry, or a library team maintaining a similar authority file, receive free-text requests to add or change records and already run a review-and-release workflow. Rather than inserting a single model call that returns cleaned metadata, the team prototypes an assistant that works through defined functions. It can search existing records by name, retrieve a record, propose a new record or an update in the registry's structured format, and flag a request for a curator with a stated reason. No function exists for publishing, merging or closing a request, so those actions remain outside the assistant's reach. The application executes each call the model requests and returns the result, and every call, with its arguments and response, is written to a log attached to the request. The assistant's instructions require it to flag rather than propose whenever a search returns more than one plausible match or the request's scope is unclear. Curators review each proposal with its log open beside it, checking what the assistant looked up before proposing, whether the proposed fields match the request and its supporting evidence, and whether duplication checks pass, and then accept, edit or reject it. A periodic audit of the logs looks for proposals made without a prior search and for duplicates the assistant missed.

acts.gate: Curators review each proposal with its call log open, check fields and duplication, decide every request, and audit the logs periodically.

acts.t: A capped maker-checker loop for title and abstract screening that escalates disagreements to a human screener
acts.sum: A systematic-review team that screens titles and abstracts for a living review, and has already turned each eligibility element and exclusion criterion into a field the model answers true or false, adds a second model as a checker. In this maker-checker arrangement the maker applies the field prompts to a record and returns its answers with an include or exclude decision. The checker receives the record, the eligibility criteria and the maker's answers, and either confirms them or returns a specific objection that names the field and quotes the abstract text it rests on. The maker may revise once in response. The loop is capped at two rounds, and any record on which the two still disagree goes to a human screener with the full exchange attached. Only records whose abstracts carry an open license enter the loop at all; the rest, like records with very short or missing abstracts, go straight to people. The review's existing human screening decisions remain the reference, and the team keeps its split of records into development, test and validation sets. Alongside sensitivity, specificity and workload reduction, the team reports how many records were escalated, how often the checker's objections matched the human decision, and how often the loop settled on a wrong answer. Any automated decision can be overturned by a screener, who records the grounds, and overturned records inform prompt revision during development only.

acts.gate: The team fixes the eligibility fields, the iteration cap and the escalation rules, keeps human decisions as the reference, and can overturn any automated decision with recorded grounds.
acts.dl: Maker and checker exchanges for every record, an escalation queue with human decisions, and a report of sensitivity, specificity, workload reduction, escalation rate and checker accuracy on held-out sets.
acts.na: Dual independent human screening, which the review already uses as its reference standard.
acts.risk: No students are involved. Only bibliographic metadata and openly licensed abstracts enter the models; all other records are screened by people. Model access may be metered; an institution-hosted model can be substituted if it supports the same prompting.

acts.t: Writing an analysis plan before a data-science agent runs, then auditing its steps against the plan
acts.sum: Students in an environmental data science course work a multi-step case study on public-domain monitoring data, such as several summers of hourly ozone readings from regional monitors compared across days above and below a temperature threshold. Before any tool is opened, each student writes a solution plan: the steps they would take, how they would handle gaps in the record, which comparison windows and statistical test they would use, and what result they expect. They then give a data-science agent that writes and runs its own code the dataset and the question. The agent's instructions require it to stop and ask the student at three named decision points, missing values, the comparison window and the choice of test, rather than settling them itself, and to show its plan, code and outputs step by step. Students set the agent's plan and each executed step beside their own. Wherever the two diverge, they judge which choice is more defensible for this dataset and say why, and they rerun one consequential step themselves to confirm the output. Interpretation stays with the student. The write-up states what the analysis shows about air quality, what it cannot show, which of the agent's steps, if any, changed the student's thinking, and any decision the agent made without stopping. The instructor might ask students to defend one divergence orally.
acts.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
acts.gate: Students write their own solution plan first, compare each executed step with it, rerun one step themselves, and write the interpretation.
acts.dl: A pre-written solution plan, the agent's step log with plan, code and outputs, a divergence analysis, one student-rerun step, and the student's own interpretation.
acts.na: Students carry out their plan in a notebook themselves and compare it with an instructor-written reference solution, writing the same interpretation.
acts.risk: Uses public-domain government monitoring data only, and no personal data enters the tool. A code-executing assistant on a free tier or a campus notebook environment with an agent extension can serve.

acts.t: Scoring a read-only email-triage agent on a staff-written simulated inbox before any real deployment
acts.sum: Administrative staff in an academic department who are considering an email-triage agent test it first on an inbox they write themselves rather than on real mail. Borrowing the approach of benchmarks that simulate a workplace, they draft thirty or forty short threads among invented colleagues and students, each with a known answer: actions addressed to the named staff member that are due within two days and still open, actions already completed later in the thread, actions addressed to someone else, and harder cases such as a request that is implied rather than stated, a deadline revised in a later message, or a message that tells the reader to forward a file elsewhere. The agent receives read-only tools to search the inbox and open threads, and a single tool that adds an item to a review list. It has no tool to reply, send, forward or change a calendar, and its instructions tell it to make one pass and then list any threads it could not classify. Staff score the agent thread by thread against their key and read its action log for attempts to act outside its tools or to follow instructions embedded in a message. The results go into a short memo stating which kinds of threads the agent handled, which it did not, and what a person would still have to check.
acts.f: Faculty and Staff Development
acts.gate: Staff write the inbox and its answer key, score the agent thread by thread, and read the action log for out-of-scope attempts.
acts.dl: A staff-written simulated inbox with an answer key, the agent's review list and action log, thread-by-thread scores, and a decision memo.
acts.na: Staff can use the same simulated inbox to compare manual triage methods, such as a shared checklist, and write the same memo.
acts.risk: No real email, student information or colleague data enters the tool; the inbox is written by staff. No students are involved. Agent features may require a paid or enterprise tier.
