acts.t: Verifying acoustic species detections before they become occurrence records in a distribution model
acts.sum: An ecology lab that has deployed autonomous sound recorders across a study region wants occurrence records for a distribution model of one bird or amphibian species. A pretrained acoustic detector, of the deep-learning kind reviewed in the bioacoustics literature, labels candidate vocalizations in the recordings, each with a confidence score. Before any detection becomes an occurrence record, the researcher draws a sample of detections at several confidence thresholds, stratified by recording site and habitat, listens to each clip, and records an expert label; a second listener checks a subset. This yields precision at each threshold and shows whether errors cluster at particular sites, for example where a similar-sounding species or persistent noise is common. Following a published species-distribution workflow, the researcher then builds a presence-background distribution model twice, once from all detections above a default threshold and once from verified detections only, keeping thinning, background extent and spatially partitioned cross-validation the same for both. Comparing the two projections shows where unverified detections shift the predicted range, and the researcher checks whether those shifts fall in conditions the training data do not cover. Working notes record which threshold and verification rate the lab will adopt, and what the final map cannot establish: where the species is absent, or why it occurs where it does.

acts.t: Pre-lab audit of a manual-grounded lab assistant using students' own questions
acts.sum: Before a remote acid-base titration, first-year chemistry students each write three questions they expect to need answered during the experiment, phrased the way they would actually type them, including at least one about a safety step and one about a calculation. The instructor has already configured a document-grounded assistant for the lab: it indexes excerpts from the course's own laboratory manual, the procedure, and the safety notes, answers only from that material with references to the sections it drew on, and is set not to supply complete numerical answers. In a pre-lab session students put their questions to the assistant and open every section it cites. For each exchange they record whether the cited passage is the right part of the manual, whether the answer says what that passage says, whether the needed passage was never retrieved at all, and whether the assistant held to its limit on calculations or let a worked number through. Oddly worded questions and questions about steps the manual covers only briefly receive particular attention. Groups pool their records into a class tally that separates retrieval errors from answer errors, and the instructor reads the tally as evidence about both the assistant's configuration and the manual itself, revising either before the lab runs. During the experiment the assistant remains optional, and students carry their tallies with them as a guide to which kinds of question it handled well.

acts.dl: Each student's three questions with the assistant's answers and cited sections; a classification of each exchange (right passage and right answer, right passage and wrong answer, wrong passage, nothing retrieved, constraint breached); and a pooled class tally that the instructor uses to revise the configuration or the manual.
acts.na: Students trade questions with a partner who answers from the manual with page references, and the class tallies which questions the manual answers clearly, poorly, or not at all.
acts.risk: Runs on the lab platform's instructor-configured assistant, so students need no personal account or paid tool; the indexed material is the instructor's own manual and safety notes. Consulting the assistant during the lab stays optional.

acts.t: Library staff chunk service documents for a retrieval assistant and log its failures by type
acts.sum: Library staff preparing a retrieval assistant for the library's own service documents, such as loan policies, room-booking rules, and interlibrary-loan procedures written by staff, begin by assembling a fixed set of questions patrons actually ask, drawn from desk logs with identifying details removed, and noting for each the passage that answers it. A generative assistant then breaks each document into short, self-contained topical chunks that name their subject. Staff read every chunk against its source paragraph and correct merged facts, dropped conditions, and wording the source does not contain. Both versions, the raw documents and the checked chunks, are indexed, and the question set is run against each. For every answer, staff open the passages the assistant cites and code what went wrong, if anything, using the seven failure points from an engineering study of deployed retrieval systems: the answer was never in the documents, the right passage ranked too low, it was retrieved but left out of the answer's context, it was present but not extracted, the format was wrong, the answer was too general or too specific, or it was incomplete. The team compares the two failure profiles, decides which documents need rewriting rather than re-chunking, and repeats the run after changes, keeping each coded log as a record of how the assistant behaved on the library's own material before it is offered to anyone.

acts.dl: A staff-checked set of topical chunks, a coded failure log for each indexing approach, a comparison of the two failure profiles, and a list of documents flagged for rewriting.
acts.na: Staff run the same question set as a findability test of the documents themselves, timing how long a colleague unfamiliar with the policies takes to locate each answer.
acts.risk: Uses staff-written documents and de-identified desk questions only; no patron data enters the tool. Requires an institution-provided assistant that supports indexing.

acts.t: Checking a source-grounded answer to a pharmacology case for support and for the right kind of source
acts.sum: In a formative undergraduate pharmacology task, the instructor indexes a small source set in a document-grounded assistant: the instructor's own mechanism notes, openly licensed treatment guideline summaries, and public-domain product labeling where it is available. Students put an instructor-written case question to the assistant, such as whether a given anticoagulant suits an older adult with reduced kidney function, and save the answer with the passages it cites. They pick out the claims that bear on safety and ask two questions of each: whether the cited passage actually says what the answer says, and whether the passage comes from the kind of source the claim needs, with mechanism claims drawn from the course notes, product safety from labeling, and treatment choice from guidelines. A correct-sounding claim cited to the wrong kind of source is logged as a retrieval error, separate from a claim the passage does not support. Students then set the assistant's answer aside and work out the mechanism on their own, tracing how the drug's target leads to its intended effect, to its risks, and to what needs monitoring, and testing that reasoning against the patient's details. They revise the answer and add a short correction note naming what changed and which source or case detail justified it. The class compares logs to see whether retrieval errors cluster around particular questions or source types, a pattern the instructor can use to adjust the packet.

acts.t: Testing whether paper order changes an assistant's critique of a trainee's literature synthesis
acts.sum: A research trainee reads each paper for a short review closely, annotates it with questions and first interpretations, and writes a synthesis across the set before consulting any AI tool; the set is drawn from openly licensed articles. Only then does the trainee give an assistant the full text of all the papers directly in a single request, without building an index or a retrieval step, together with the synthesis, and ask it to identify omissions and misrepresentations. Because a study of long inputs reports that models use material placed in the middle less reliably than material at the start or end, the trainee runs the same request a second time with the papers in a different order, moving the paper the trainee considers most important from first position to the middle of the set. Every gap or misreading the assistant flags in either run is checked against the original text and marked as confirmed, already addressed, or not supported by the paper. The trainee then compares the two critiques: which flags appear in only one run, and whether those concern papers that sat in the middle. A short note records which confirmed gaps led to revisions and what the comparison suggests about relying on a single critique of a long input. The synthesis remains the trainee's own work throughout; the assistant's role is to point at places worth rereading, and no paper is cited that the trainee has not read.

acts.na: A peer who has read the same papers critiques the synthesis for omissions, and the trainee checks each comment against the papers in the same way.
acts.risk: Input-length limits differ between free and paid tiers; with shorter limits the trainee can supply fewer or shorter papers or use institution-provided access. acts.t: Testing an assistant's themes in an open management textbook before writing discussion questions
acts.sum: In an upper-level management course, the assigned reading is a set of sections from an openly licensed management textbook. Before any AI use, each student skims the sections and lists the three or four themes they expect to matter most. A document-grounded assistant that indexes the same sections is then asked for the major themes, with references to the passages each theme rests on. Students open every cited passage and decide whether it carries the theme or whether a single passing mention has been inflated into one. They also look for a theme from their own list that the assistant did not return, rephrase the request once or twice to see whether a narrower question retrieves it, and record whether the missing theme reflects a retrieval miss or a genuine difference in reading. Only themes that survive this check feed the next stage. In small groups students generate as many discussion questions as they can for each verified theme, treating none as unworthy at first, then sort and rank them and select the few the group will bring to class, each tied to a specific passage. A one-page summary in the student's own words accompanies the questions, and the class discussion proceeds from the student-written questions, with time set aside to compare which themes the assistant overweighted or missed.

acts.t: Editing an instructor-generated, citation-bearing text against the course readings
acts.sum: The instructor indexes the course readings that are openly licensed or instructor-written in a document-grounded assistant and uses it to generate a short text, perhaps six hundred words, on a topic the class has studied, asking for inline citations to those readings. Students receive the printed text and the readings; they do not use the tool themselves. Working as editors in a document with tracked changes, they audit the text sentence by sentence in two directions that the citation literature distinguishes. For every sentence that makes a claim, is it fully supported by the passages it cites? For every citation, does the cited passage support the sentence it is attached to, or is it merely on the same topic? Students tally both, so the text receives two simple counts alongside their comments. They then correct factual and theoretical errors, add context from the readings where a sentence has no support or the wrong support, and develop the argument with cases of their own. A closing paragraph describes the assumptions about class, gender, race, and ability that the original carried, including any that the readings themselves do not support. Before submitting, students compare their two counts with the instructor's own audit of the same text and write a few sentences on where their judgment differed and why. The marked-up, expanded text is the submission, read against the course readings and class discussion.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Students audit every sentence for citation support and every citation for relevance, correct errors, add missing context from the readings, analyze embedded assumptions, and calibrate their audit against the instructor's.
acts.dl: A tracked-changes edit of the generated text with comments, a sentence-level support count and a citation-level relevance count, an added paragraph on embedded assumptions, and a short calibration note comparing the student's counts with the instructor's.
acts.na: The instructor writes or adapts a short cited text containing deliberate citation errors, and students apply the same two counts and edits.
acts.risk: Students need no account or tool. Only openly licensed or instructor-written course readings are indexed; copyrighted readings stay out of the tool and can still be used by students when they add context in their edits.

acts.t: Faculty build a closed course assistant and rate it with a typed question set
acts.sum: Participants in an accredited certificate in teaching and learning have already read an article unaided and compared their reading with a machine summary. In this unit each participant builds a closed course assistant, using a no-code builder that indexes documents they supply: openly licensed or self-authored readings, their own slides, and a course-information page with deadlines and policies. Before trying it, each participant writes a question set of perhaps twenty items in three types: questions about content in the readings, questions that require connecting two readings, and organizational questions about dates, submission, and policies. The questions are put to the assistant and the answers saved. Pairs then rate each other's answer sets independently, marking each answer as correct and supported, partly correct, or wrong, and noting whether the cited passage was the one a student would need. Partners compare ratings, discuss the answers on which they disagreed, and record why agreement came harder on open-ended content questions than on factual or organizational ones, if it did. Each participant summarizes how the assistant performed by question type, revises the documents or configuration where answers failed, and closes with a reflection on whether, and for which kinds of question, they would release such an assistant to their own students, and what students would need to know about its limits.

acts.na: Participants exchange course documents and answer each other's question sets from the documents alone, rating the findability and clarity of the materials instead.
acts.risk: Requires an institution-provided no-code assistant builder; only openly licensed or self-authored materials are indexed, and no student data is used.

acts.t: Tracing a famous quotation through a searchable corpus of the attributed author's public-domain works
acts.sum: Students choose a well-known quotation attributed to a writer or public figure whose works are in the public domain, and record whom it is usually credited to and where they have seen it. They then trace it through three channels. The top results of an ordinary web search give one answer. A document-grounded assistant, into which the librarian has indexed the attributed author's collected works from public-domain digital editions, gives another: students ask it where the words appear and save the passages it returns with their references. Because this kind of retrieval matches meaning rather than exact wording, it can return a passage that resembles the quotation in idea without containing it, so students check every returned passage with an exact-phrase search of the same text files and classify it as a verbatim match, a close paraphrase, a related idea, or nothing that supports the attribution. A passage the assistant presents as the source is never accepted on its word. Where nothing matches, students treat the absence as a finding to be tested rather than proof, searching a few distinctive words and checking letters or speeches the edition may not include. They finish with a verified or corrected attribution and a short account of what the search results, the assistant, and the primary text each said, including any passage the assistant offered that did not hold up.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Students check every returned passage by exact-phrase search of the same files and classify it as verbatim match, close paraphrase, related idea, or no support for the attribution.
acts.dl: A verified or corrected attribution, a table of passages returned by the assistant with each one's classification, the exact-phrase search results, and a short account comparing the three channels.
acts.na: Students trace the quotation through web search, a quotation dictionary, and exact-phrase search of the public-domain texts, and compare the three answers with the starting attribution.
acts.risk: Works only with public-domain editions, so no copyrighted text enters the tool; the librarian prepares the index, and students need only access to it and to the text files.

acts.t: Transferring a public-domain painting's style onto a student photograph and tracing who made which part
acts.sum: Students choose a photograph they took themselves and two or three paintings in the public domain, which the instructor may tie to course themes, and run them through a neural style-transfer notebook that rebuilds the photograph so its content stays recognizable while its textures and colors follow a painting. Over several runs they change the balance between content and style and the network layers used, saving each output with its settings. For the result they find most interesting, they make an annotated map that attributes each visible feature: composition and objects to their photograph, brushwork and palette to the painting, and artifacts such as repeated textures or smeared edges to the optimization itself. Each student shares the final image beside its sources, labeled as a style-transfer output, together with the map and an account of the choices made. A group discussion then asks who authored the result: the student who chose and tuned, the painter whose manner was measured and copied, or the procedure. It also takes up what it means to imitate an artist's manner even when the work is in the public domain, how the tool's division of an image into content and style shapes what students notice, and when an artist or designer might use such a process or decline to.
acts.f: Co-Authoring with AI: Voice and Authorship
acts.gate: Students vary the content-style balance and layers, then map which features of the result come from the photograph, the painting, or the optimization.
acts.dl: A labeled style-transfer image shown with its source photograph and painting, a log of settings, an annotated attribution map, and the group's discussion notes.
acts.na: Students can make a hand-painted or collaged study of their photograph in a public-domain painter's manner and produce the same attribution map.
acts.risk: Only students' own photographs and public-domain paintings are entered; a photograph that shows an identifiable person is used only with that person's consent. The instructor can run the notebook for students without a suitable device. Shared outputs carry image descriptions.

acts.t: Predicting colors for public-domain historical photographs, then testing a colorization model's choices against documentary evidence
acts.sum: Building on readings about how image models produce statistically typical pictures, students select black-and-white photographs from public-domain collections, showing things such as uniforms, storefronts, vehicles, textiles or painted signs. Before any processing they write down the colors they expect a colorization model to assign and the colors they believe the objects actually had. Each student then colorizes the photograph twice, once with no guidance and once with a short text description, logging every prompt, saving every output, and labeling each as colorized. The research half follows. For each object the student looks for documentary evidence of its color, such as regulations, trade catalogs, paint or dye records, written descriptions from the period, surviving artifacts in museum collections, or early color photographs. Every color choice is marked as supported by evidence, contradicted by it, or not determinable, with the source cited. Groups compare these results with their predictions and across students working on similar subjects, noting where the model defaulted to modern or generic palettes, how skin and fabric were handled, and where a text description overrode the evidence. A shared document collects telling examples, and a debrief returns to the readings to ask what a colorized photograph adds to the historical record and what it takes away.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Students research documentary evidence for each colored object and mark the model's choice as supported, contradicted or not determinable.
acts.dl: Written predictions, two labeled colorized versions with logs, an object-by-object evidence table with citations, and a shared group document of examples.
acts.na: Students can hand-tint a printed copy of the photograph from their predictions and run the same evidence check on their own color choices.
acts.risk: Only public-domain photographs are entered, and every output is labeled as colorized. Evidence tables use named colors, which supports students with color-vision differences.

acts.t: Auditing generated card art for a global health trade game for nationality stereotypes before play
acts.sum: An instructor and teaching assistant building a classroom card game in which fifteen states trade resources and weather events that affect their populations' health generate the art for resource and event cards with a text-to-image model, aiming for generic images without identifiable people or places. Before the game reaches students, the card set is audited with the method of a published study of nationality stereotypes in generated images. The team first separates traits that can be seen in an image, such as clothing, housing, landscape and transport, from traits that cannot, and writes a short list of visible attributes that would amount to a stereotype for each region represented. A panel, which can include volunteers from a previous offering, annotates every card for those attributes without knowing which state it was generated for. The tallies are then compared across states: do one region's cards show dirt roads, crowding or traditional dress far more often than others, and do plain prompts pull certain states toward the same few images? Cards that carry a stereotype are regenerated with revised prompts, replaced with simple icons, or dropped, and each change is logged. When the game is played, students meet the change log in the debrief and discuss whether and how generic prompts still produced a patterned picture of the world's health.
acts.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
acts.gate: A blind panel annotates every card for listed visual stereotype attributes, tallies are compared across states, and flagged cards are revised, replaced or dropped.
acts.dl: An annotated audit of every card with tallies by state, a revised card set with generated images labeled, and a change log used in the students' debrief.
acts.na: The game can use icon-only cards or openly licensed photographs, and the same blind audit can be run on that set.
acts.risk: Students do not use AI. Generated images are labeled and depict no identifiable people or places; panel volunteers are not graded. Cards carry text labels so play does not depend on reading the images.

acts.t: Generating identity-label portraits in two languages and setting them beside archival portraits of the same categories
acts.sum: Groups with access to a second language, whether through a member who speaks it or a language the course teaches, pick a few identity labels that carry social or political weight, for example nurse, migrant worker or engineer, and record the assumptions commonly attached to each. For every label they write prompts in English and in the second language, and where that language marks grammatical gender, in a masculine form, a feminine form and a gender-neutral rephrasing, following the design of a multilingual benchmark study. They generate the same number of portraits for each version with one text-to-image platform, record the platform and settings, and label every image as generated. Each portrait is coded for perceived gender presentation, apparent age, setting and props by two coders, with disagreements noted rather than settled by guesswork. Groups then gather existing portraits of the same categories from openly licensed art-history, news and archival collections and code them the same way, so the generated sets can be compared with the visual history they may draw on. The analysis asks whether the language of the prompt shifted the images, whether neutral phrasing changed anything, and whether the generator repeats or intensifies typologies already present in the archive. Groups present their comparison and write a reflection connecting the tallies to the course's readings on faces and recognition technology.
acts.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
acts.gate: Two coders per image record perceived gender presentation, apparent age, setting and props; tallies are compared across languages and with an archival set.

acts.risk: Generated faces show no real person; archival portraits come only from openly licensed collections and are never entered into a tool. Codes record perceived presentation only, and groups discuss the limits of coding gender from images.

acts.t: Training a paired image-translation model on the studio's own facade drawings and photographs, then critiquing what it invents
acts.sum: In an architectural design studio, students move from describing facades to building the data a model learns from. Each student photographs a set of campus and neighborhood facades from public streets, framing them straight on, and draws a matching label map by hand in which flat colors stand for wall, window, door, cornice and so on, following a legend the studio agrees. The pooled pairs become a training set for the paired image-translation notebook, which a technical instructor runs and adapts, setting aside some buildings the model never sees. The trained model then renders facades from label maps: first those of the held-out buildings, so its output can be set beside the real photograph, and then new label maps that students draw as design proposals. In studio crits each rendering is examined against the photograph and the label map, asking which elements the model reproduced, which it invented, such as mullions, ornament or weathering, and where it blurred a deliberate design move into a typical facade. Discussion also takes up how the class's own choice of buildings shaped what the model treats as normal. Every rendering is labeled as a model output, and students keep a log of the outputs they accepted and rejected, with reasons, which feeds the studio's discussion of authorship and accountability.
acts.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
acts.gate: In studio crits, students compare each rendering with the held-out photograph and their label map and mark what the model invented or smoothed away.
acts.dl: A shared paired dataset with its label legend, a trained model, renderings of held-out and proposed facades, crit notes, and a log of accepted and rejected outputs with reasons.
acts.na: Students can render one another's label maps by hand and hold the same crit, comparing interpretations across people instead of against a model.
acts.risk: Photographs are taken by students from public streets and avoid people; training runs on institutional computing managed by the technical instructor, so students need no account or paid service.

acts.t: Restoring the image of a water-damaged in-house manual page while marking every reconstructed region
acts.sum: A library unit's only printed copy of an in-house procedure binder, written by its own staff, has been water-damaged, and the photographs taken for digitization show stains, tears and faded diagram lines. Staff use an inpainting model to restore the page images so they can be read and reprinted, under rules that keep every generated detail identifiable. Before any processing, a staff member marks on each photograph the regions that may be filled, such as background stains, margins and broken lines in simple diagrams, and excludes every area containing text, numbers or labels, since the model would supply plausible characters that were never there. Text in damaged areas is instead transcribed by a person from the original page or marked as illegible. After restoration, the filled regions are saved as a separate mask layer, so anyone can switch between the original and the restored image, and a diagram that cannot be reconstructed with confidence is labeled as such rather than redrawn. Colleagues who actually perform the procedure then review each restored page against the damaged original and their own knowledge of the steps, confirming or rejecting each filled region. The archived version keeps the original photographs, the restored images, the masks and a processing note.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Staff mask which regions may be filled, exclude all text, and have the people who perform the procedure confirm or reject each filled region.
acts.dl: Restored page images with a separate mask layer of every filled region, human transcriptions or illegibility labels for damaged text, a staff review record, and a processing note.
acts.na: Staff can retype the binder and redraw diagrams by hand from the damaged pages, with the same illegibility labels and review.
acts.risk: Only the library's own in-house document is processed; manufacturer or other third-party manuals are not entered. The retyped text produced alongside the images makes the procedure available to screen-reader users.

acts.t: Asking an image generator to draw your data, then auditing its chart against a figure plotted from the data
acts.sum: In a short research-integrity workshop, researchers bring a small table of their own non-sensitive data and a description of the figure they intend to make from it. Each participant first asks a code-generation assistant for plotting code, reads it until they can vouch for every line, runs it, and saves the resulting figure with the code and the data source. Then, as a test rather than a production step, they give an image generator the same values and the same description and ask it to draw the figure. The two figures are laid side by side and the generated one is audited mark by mark: values that do not match the table, axis ranges and tick labels that were changed or invented, legend entries for series that do not exist, error bars that were never supplied, and lettering that reads plausibly but says nothing. Participants tally what they find and share examples. Discussion links the tally to publisher policies that treat generated or manipulated images in papers as misconduct, and to why a figure that can be regenerated from code and data can be disclosed and checked in a way a picture cannot. Each participant leaves with the reproducible figure, its code, and a disclosure statement for the delegated coding task, while the generated chart is labeled and kept only as a workshop specimen.
acts.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
acts.gate: The researcher compares every value, axis, tick label, legend entry and error bar in the generated chart with the figure plotted by code from the same table.
acts.dl: A code-plotted figure with its code and data source, a labeled generated chart, a mark-by-mark audit tally, and a disclosure statement for the coding assistance.
acts.na: Participants can audit an instructor-prepared generated chart against its source table and write the plotting code themselves.
acts.risk: Only the participant's own non-sensitive or synthetic data is entered, and the generated chart is never used in publication. Final figures carry alt text and the data table for screen-reader users.

acts.t: Keeping a student-drawn character consistent across a generated picture book and logging where it drifts
acts.sum: Pre-service teachers producing a short picture book for young readers begin by writing the story and drawing their main character themselves, in a few poses on plain paper, with a short list of features that should not change, such as the shape of the ears, the pattern on a coat, or a missing tooth. They then use an image generator that accepts a small set of reference images of a subject, supplying only their own drawings, and generate the scenes the story needs, saving every prompt and every unedited output. For each page they check the character against the feature list and log each drift: a coat that changes color, an extra finger, an age shift, a face sliding toward a generic cartoon style, or features that change when the setting changes. For each scene they decide whether to accept it, regenerate it, redraw it by hand, or cut it, and record why. Text and selected images are laid out into a draft book of about twelve pages, with the cover stating which images were generated from the student's drawings. The assessed product is the process portfolio of drawings, feature list, prompts, unedited outputs and drift log, together with a reflective essay on authorship, on what consistency means for a child reader, and on the university's AI guidance.
acts.f: Co-Authoring with AI: Voice and Authorship
acts.gate: Students log every drift in the character's listed features across pages and decide which outputs to accept, regenerate, redraw or cut.
acts.dl: Hand-drawn reference sheets and a feature list, saved prompts and unedited outputs, a page-by-page drift log, a draft picture book with labeled images, and a reflective essay.
acts.na: Students can illustrate every scene by hand, or trade reference sheets with a peer who illustrates them, and log drift the same way.
acts.risk: Only the student's own drawings are used as references; no real person's likeness or existing commercial character is entered. Students who do not draw can make cut-paper or collage references.

acts.t: Mapping where data goes during a training job in the institution's managed machine-learning environment
acts.sum: Graduate students in science and engineering who take a research-ethics course before submitting a proposal add a hands-on component to its unit on AI ethics. Individually or in small groups, they train and tune a small predictive model on a public-domain or instructor-supplied dataset inside the managed machine-learning environment that the institution's research computing group provisions for the class, following an open workshop's sequence of storage, notebooks, training jobs, tuning and resource monitoring. While they work, students draw a data-movement map: every place the data or a derivative of it is copied, which region it sits in, which institutional roles can read it, what persists after the job ends, and what the resource meter records. They then carry the map into the ethics case they chose, for example the misuse of personal data from a dating site, and ask what the same handling would have looked like if that case's data had passed through this environment. The written product is the data-management section of a mock research proposal. It analyzes the students' own workflow at the level of the underlying technology, the specific configured system and its use in a research project, and addresses anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion and responsiveness. A short comparison with running the same training on a laptop, where feasible, closes the section.

acts.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse

acts.na: Students can map the documented data flow of the open workshop's example environment from its lesson pages and apply it to the ethics case without running a job.
acts.risk: Research computing provisions class access, so students need no personal cloud account and pay nothing. Only public-domain or instructor-supplied data is used, and no personal data enters the environment. Quotas set by the institution bound resource use.

acts.t: Turning a business ethics privacy question on the institution's own licensed AI service
acts.sum: In a business ethics unit on technology, students finish the assigned readings and, before any AI use, draft their own responses to a pair of workplace privacy questions. They then put the same questions to the institution's licensed AI assistant, which they reach through campus sign-in under the institution's agreement rather than through a personal consumer account, cite the response, and judge how well it answered and what grade it would earn. The second half of the assignment turns the unit's questions on the tool itself. Using the institution's published description of its AI service, and the terms of the agreement where they are public, students work out what happened to what they just typed: whether it is retained and for how long, whether it may be used to train models, which institutional roles can see logs, and what a consumer version of a similar tool would have done differently. They evaluate that arrangement with the same ethical frameworks they applied in their written answers, and say whether their own answer to the privacy questions changes now that they are, in effect, the employees whose inputs are governed by an employer's contract. Answers, chatbot outputs and evaluations are shared with the course, and discussion extends to what students would require of a vendor in their intended careers.
acts.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
acts.gate: Students write their own answers before using the assistant, grade its answer against theirs, and then establish from institutional documents what happened to their own inputs.
acts.dl: Two written answers, the cited chatbot response with a grade and rationale, an evaluation of the institution's AI-service data terms, and discussion posts.
acts.na: Students can analyze the institution's published AI-service description and a consumer service's terms without using either tool, and answer the same privacy questions.
acts.risk: Students use institutional sign-in and need no personal account or payment. Students are asked not to enter personal information about themselves or others. Where the institution has not published service terms, the instructor might obtain a summary from the IT office.

acts.t: Evaluating a reference assistant grounded in the library's own documentation inside the institution's environment
acts.sum: A reference librarian who wants to know whether a document-grounded assistant could help answer the library's email questions adapts a published method for scoring a general chatbot on real reference questions, changing where the system runs and what it reads. Email questions the library received during a chosen period are collected, stripped of personal and confidential details, and sorted by type and by the effort level they demand. The library's systems partner configures a retrieval-grounded assistant inside the institution's own cloud environment, indexing only the library's public web pages and internal service documentation on hours, borrowing, interlibrary loan and access problems. Before any question is run, the librarian and the systems partner map every data transfer in the arrangement, from document ingestion to the query path, logs and retention, and confirm that question text stays within the institution's environment. Each question then goes to the assistant, and every answer is rated at three levels for how complete and how accurate it is and whether it points the user to further help, with accuracy checked by reference colleagues and a note on whether the answer cited a local page. The analysis pays particular attention to local, complex and access questions, the categories where the published evaluation found a general chatbot weakest. A short memo for library leadership addresses need, process, results, unintended outcomes and the cost of keeping the index current.
acts.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
acts.gate: Librarians map every data transfer before testing, then score each answer on the rubric with accuracy confirmed by colleagues against current policies and pages.
acts.dl: A de-identified, typed question set, a data-transfer map of the assistant, rubric scores for every answer with notes on local citations, and an evaluation memo.
acts.na: The librarian can score the library's existing answer templates or FAQ pages against the same question set and rubric to find gaps in documentation.
acts.risk: No patron uses the assistant during the evaluation, and de-identified questions are processed inside the institution's environment. The work requires a systems partner with access to an institutional cloud tenancy.

acts.t: Scoping an enterprise assistant to instructor-authored files before it drafts discussion questions from public-domain readings
acts.sum: An instructor preparing an upper-division course on nature writing, built on public-domain and openly licensed readings rather than a textbook, uses the institution's licensed AI assistant to draft discussion questions, and first deals with a feature of enterprise deployment: the assistant can draw on any file the instructor's account can open. For many instructors that includes earlier students' submissions saved in cloud storage, colleagues' shared drafts and committee papers. Working with IT or library staff, the instructor builds a folder holding only the course readings, the outcomes document and their own lecture notes, and restricts the assistant to that folder where the tool allows it. A short test question about the course, read alongside the file references the assistant attaches to its answer, shows whether the restriction holds. The instructor then prompts iteratively for questions tied to named outcomes. Every question is checked twice: against the reading, for a page or passage it points to and for claims the text does not make, and against the files the assistant cites, so that any question drawing on something outside the folder is discarded and the gap reported to IT. Questions that fail either check are dropped or rewritten. The instructor tells students how the questions were produced and what the assistant was allowed to read, and shares the folder setup with colleagues.
acts.f: Designing Courses and Learning Materials with AI
acts.gate: The instructor narrows what the assistant may read, tests that the restriction holds, and checks every question against the reading and against the files the assistant cites.
acts.dl: A scoped source folder, a recorded test of the restriction, a passage-checked and reference-checked set of discussion questions tied to course outcomes, and a short setup note for colleagues.
acts.na: The instructor writes discussion questions from their own reading of the texts, using the same list of outcomes.
acts.risk: Students do not use the assistant and nothing they have written is meant to enter it; the scoping step and reference check exist to keep earlier students' work out. Where the assistant cannot be restricted to the folder, earlier students' work may remain within its reach, so a course that needs to guarantee that no student text enters a tool can use the non-AI route. Only public-domain or openly licensed readings and instructor-written notes are supplied.

acts.t: Testing an enterprise-licensed and an institution-hosted model on accreditation evidence mapping against a preset threshold
acts.sum: An accreditation and assessment office that wants to know whether AI can help map evidence artifacts to accreditation standards tests the two deployments the institution has approved, rather than whichever tool is at hand. Staff first select nonsensitive artifacts that policy allows for the test, leaving out any candidate-authored work, and two experts code each one against the codebook independently and reconcile their differences; that reconciled coding is the reference. Before any model runs, the office sets the agreement level a deployment would need to reach before its labels could be used for anything beyond suggestions, following the practice of fixing an automation threshold in advance. The same artifacts and instructions then go to the institution's enterprise-licensed assistant and to an open-weight model the institution hosts on its own servers. The comparison matters for a practical reason. Some evidence the office routinely handles, such as samples of candidates' coursework, may be processed only on the hosted model under the institution's data policy, so the hosted model's accuracy on the test set decides whether AI has any role with those materials. Agreement with the expert coding is reported at the finer criterion level and the broader standard level for each deployment, and disagreements are reviewed one by one. The office records its decision, with the reasons, in its governance documentation.
acts.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
acts.gate: Experts code first and reconcile, the office fixes an agreement threshold before any model runs, and every model label and disagreement is checked against the reconciled coding.
acts.dl: A reconciled expert coding of the test artifacts, a preset agreement threshold, criterion- and standard-level agreement figures for each deployment, a disagreement review, and a recorded governance decision.
acts.na: The office continues expert coding alone, which the test uses as its reference in any case.
acts.risk: Only nonsensitive artifacts the institution's policy permits for testing are used, with no candidate-authored work in the test set, and only within approved deployments; any later use with candidates' coursework is a separate governance decision. The hosted model requires institutional infrastructure; no one is asked to use a personal account.

acts.t: Checking a draft peer review on a local, offline model while the manuscript stays out of every tool
acts.sum: A faculty member who has drafted a review for a journal or conference wants a check on the review's own quality, but the review is part of a confidential process and many editorial policies prohibit sending reviews or manuscripts to outside AI services. Following an open course's appendix on running language models locally, the reviewer installs an openly available model on their own computer and works with the network connection switched off, after confirming that the venue's reviewer policy allows local use of this kind and noting how it would be disclosed if asked. Only the reviewer's own draft review goes to the model; the manuscript stays out of every tool. Drawing on the published design of a review-feedback pipeline, the reviewer runs three checks in turn: comments that are vague or generic, remarks that read as unprofessional, and a list of every question the review puts to the authors. The third check is completed by hand. The reviewer takes each listed question back to the manuscript and marks it as genuinely open or already answered, with the page. Each flag is treated as a suggestion, and because a local model is smaller than those the pipeline was built on, the reviewer also notes flags that are wrong or trivial. The reviewer then revises, or does not, and keeps a brief note of which flags led to changes.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: The reviewer checks each flag and each listed question against the manuscript by reading it, decides whether to revise, and records which flags were wrong or trivial.
acts.dl: A revised review, a record of each flag with the reviewer's decision, a question list marked open or already answered with manuscript pages, and a note of false or trivial flags.
acts.na: The reviewer can apply the same three checks as a self-review checklist, or ask a co-reviewer to read the draft review where the venue allows.
acts.risk: Requires a computer able to run a small local model; the software and models are free. Local configuration alone does not prove that no data leaves the device, so the reviewer disables network access during the run. The manuscript, a third-party work, is never entered into any tool.

acts.t: Debriefing a hospital emergency simulation from transcripts kept under an institutional retention schedule
acts.sum: Faculty who run a role-differentiated hospital emergency simulation, in which each student takes one professional role in a hospital's response and answers in writing as the scenario escalates, host the scenario engine on the institution's managed chat service instead of a public chatbot. The institutional arrangement changes three things. Students sign in with their campus identity rather than a personal account. Each conversation is stored in institution-controlled storage under a retention period the program sets. And faculty can retrieve a student's transcript afterward. Before the simulation, students are told what is stored, who can read it, for how long, and how to request an alternative format. The faculty-configured scenario engine presents time-sensitive prompts across defined phases and ends with a role-specific debrief of its own. The faculty debrief then works from the stored transcripts. Each student's decisions are set against the scenario's escalation phases and the unit's emergency protocol, and students compare the engine's automatic debrief with the faculty one, marking where the engine praised a decision the protocol does not support or passed over a delay that mattered. Excerpts used in group discussion are shared only with the student's agreement and with names removed, and the retained transcripts are deleted at the end of the stated period.
acts.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
acts.gate: Faculty and students analyze stored transcripts against the escalation phases and emergency protocol, and students contest the engine's automatic debrief.
acts.dl: Stored simulation transcripts, a faculty debrief built on them, each student's annotated comparison of the automatic and faculty debriefs, and consented, anonymized excerpts for group discussion.
acts.na: Faculty can run the scenario as a tabletop exercise, with a faculty member presenting the escalation prompts and a note-taker recording decisions for the debrief.
acts.risk: Campus sign-in replaces personal accounts and there is no cost to students. Students are told in advance what is stored and who can see it; excerpts are shared in group debrief only with consent, and retention follows the program's stated schedule.

acts.t: Testing what data minimization costs when IEP goals are drafted on an approved hosted service
acts.sum: Preservice and in-service special educators practice drafting individualized education program goals from fictional, instructor-written student scenarios, with an added question that their future practice will raise: how much of a student's information a goal-writing tool actually needs. For the first scenario each participant writes a goal unaided. For the second, they fill in a published structured goal template in two versions and submit each to the institution's privately hosted AI service, which the program has approved and which does not retain prompts. The full version supplies every field, including the scenario's invented name and disability identification. The minimized version replaces the name with a placeholder, omits the disability category, and keeps only the present level of performance, goal area, condition, behavior, criterion and time frame. Participants then rate all three goals, the unaided one and both generated ones, on six items of a published goal-rating instrument, which look at whether the behavior a goal targets can be seen and counted, serves the student's daily functioning, carries over to new settings, and can be taught by different team members across the day, and compare ratings with a partner. A short written reflection names which fields could be left out without weakening the goal, which seemed to matter, and which they would not enter into any tool, approved or not, when the student is real. The instructor gathers the field-by-field findings across the class and shares the pattern.
acts.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
acts.gate: Participants write one goal unaided before any tool use, then rate all goals on the rubric and judge field by field what minimization cost.
acts.dl: An unaided goal, two generated goals from full and minimized templates, partner-compared rubric ratings for all three, and a reflection on which fields each goal needed.
acts.na: Participants can write the second goal twice by hand, once from the full scenario and once from the minimized fields, and rate all goals with the same rubric.

acts.t: Building a small corpus from machine-transcribed handwritten letters and tracing how transcription errors move the counts
acts.sum: Students assemble a small corpus of handwritten letters from a public-domain digitized collection, saving each page image with a file name that carries the date and writer. Before any machine processing, each student reads and transcribes one page by hand, and that transcription becomes the reference for the page. The instructor or the students then send every page image to an image-reading model with a fixed transcription instruction and keep the raw output. As in the archival study the operation comes from, they compute character and word error rates on the hand-transcribed pages, run a second correction pass on a few pages, and measure whether it helped. The corpus is loaded into a web-based counting environment twice, once as raw machine text and once with the sample pages corrected, and students work through guided questions comparing the two: which frequent words change rank, which words that seem distinctive of a writer turn out to be misreadings, how spelling variants and abbreviations were silently modernized, and what a keyword-in-context search misses when one name is transcribed three different ways. Each claim students make about a writer's vocabulary is checked against the page image of at least one occurrence. The products are the error-rate table, the paired frequency tables, and a short account of which findings survive correction.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Students hand-transcribe sample pages to measure error rates, then compare frequencies and concordances built from raw and corrected text.
acts.dl: Hand transcriptions of sample pages, an error-rate table for first-pass and corrected text, paired frequency and concordance tables, and a short account of which findings survive correction.
acts.na: Students can transcribe the corpus by hand in shares and compare two students' transcriptions of the same pages to see how transcription choices change the counts.
acts.risk: Only public-domain page images are entered, and the instructor can run the transcription so students need no account. Screen magnification helps with reading page images.

acts.t: Suggesting retention categories for scanned records with a document-reading model and comparing each suggestion with an archivist's decision
acts.sum: A university records unit testing whether a document-reading model could help sort a backlog draws on a published teaching case in which archivists compared machine classifiers with their own decisions. Archivists select a pilot batch of scanned records from the institution's own files, excluding anything containing personal or restricted information, and first assign each record to a category of the retention and disposition schedule themselves, without seeing any machine output. A staff member then gives the model each scanned record as a document, together with the schedule's category definitions, and asks for a suggested category, the passage or visual feature it relied on, and a statement when the record fits no category. The suggestions are tabulated beside the archivists' decisions. For each disagreement an archivist returns to the record and accepts, amends or rejects the suggestion, writing down the grounds and noting where layout, handwriting, stamps or attachments were misread. The team summarizes agreement by category, the kinds of records that went wrong, and whether the passages the model cited actually supported its suggestions. Retention decisions stay with archivists throughout, and the pilot report states whether the model suits a first sort, particular record series, or nothing at all, with the reasoning attached.

acts.gate: Archivists decide each record independently first, then accept, amend or reject the model's suggestion and record the grounds.
acts.dl: A table of archivists' independent decisions beside model suggestions and cited passages, a record of accepted, amended and rejected suggestions with grounds, and a pilot report.
acts.na: Archivists assign schedule categories by hand with a second archivist reviewing a sample, as in the reference condition of the parent case.
acts.risk: Only institutional records cleared for processing are used, in an institution-approved environment; restricted and personal records are excluded.

acts.t: Walking a site first, then testing an image model's segmentation of the street against field counts
acts.sum: Before designing for a site, architecture students walk the street in pairs, sketch the elevations, and record simple field counts at fixed points: trees, entrances, storefronts, parked cars, bus stops, and how much sky they can see. At the same points they take their own photographs from standing height, avoiding faces and license plates or blurring them. Back in the studio, they give the photographs to an image-understanding model and ask for segmentation masks and object locations, then compute what share of each image the model assigns to sky, vegetation, building facade, roadway and pavement, and how many entrances or trees it detects. These figures are set against the field counts and sketches point by point. Where the two disagree, students look at the mask itself and mark what went wrong: shadows labeled as road, glass facades read as sky, street trees merged with a park behind them, an entrance missed because it was recessed. Groups then decide which measures are reliable enough to include in the design brief, which need the field count instead, and which questions about the site neither source can answer, such as how the street is used at night. The discussion of model bias asks how these errors might relate to the kinds of streets represented in the model's training data.
acts.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
acts.gate: Students compare segment shares and detections with their field counts and sketches and mark mislabeled regions.
acts.dl: Field sketches and counts, segmentation masks with computed shares, a point-by-point comparison marking mislabeled regions, and a section of the design brief stating which measures were used and why.
acts.na: Students can estimate shares by laying a grid over printed photographs and counting cells, comparing the grid estimates with field counts in the same way.
acts.risk: Students use their own photographs taken from public streets, with faces and plates blurred. Pairs can divide walking and recording roles so students with mobility constraints can take part.

acts.t: Extracting DuPont inputs from a layout-heavy annual report by hand and with a document-reading model, then reconciling the two
acts.sum: Students analyzing financial statements work from an annual report the instructor has built as a PDF for a fictional company and laid out the way real reports are: income statement and balance sheet on different pages, a table continued across a page break, figures in thousands in one table and millions in another, a restated prior year in a footnote, and a chart that repeats some numbers. Each student first locates the needed figures, works out the three-part DuPont breakdown of return on equity, with its margin, turnover and leverage components, and writes an interpretation. They then give the same PDF to a document-reading model with an instruction to extract each input with its page and table, show every step of the calculation, and state its assumptions, such as whether average or year-end equity was used. Students reconcile the two analyses figure by figure. Each difference is traced to the page and classified as a misread layout, an unconverted unit, a missed restatement, a different but defensible assumption, or an error of their own. A 300-word reflection compares the two analyses and states which conclusions about the company hold under both. Because the report is fictional and instructor-written, an answer key exists, and the layout features can be varied from one term to the next.
acts.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
acts.gate: Students extract and compute by hand first, then reconcile every figure and step with the model's, tracing each difference to the page.
acts.dl: A hand-computed DuPont analysis and interpretation, the model's step-by-step extraction and calculation, a figure-by-figure reconciliation with classified differences, and a 300-word reflection.
acts.na: Students can exchange hand analyses with a partner and reconcile them the same way, using the answer key as the final reference.
acts.risk: The report is fictional and instructor-written, so no third-party filing is entered into a tool. The PDF is tagged for screen readers with tables marked up.

acts.t: Asking an image-reading model to assess a documented nineteenth-century photographic hoax, with and without the caption
acts.sum: Each student chooses a documented photographic hoax from the nineteenth or early twentieth century whose images are in the public domain, such as the spirit photographs exposed in court in the 1860s, and researches how it was made and how it was exposed. They then test an image-reading model as a would-be verifier. In the first run the photograph goes in cropped of any caption or label, with a request to describe what is shown and say whether there are signs of manipulation. In the second, the same image goes in with its catalog caption. Students go through both responses one statement at a time and mark each as visible in the image, not visible, or supplied from elsewhere, paying particular attention to objects, attributes and relations the model describes that are not there, and to claims about the photographer or technique that appear only once the caption is given. A short in-class presentation compares the model's two accounts with the documented history of the hoax. Discussion follows on what was hardest to check, whether a model that recognizes a famous image is seeing it or remembering it, how this compares with earlier manipulation and its exposure, and whether and by whom image-reading tools should be relied on for verification.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Students mark each statement in both responses as visible in the image, not visible, or supplied from elsewhere, and compare with the documented history.
acts.dl: Two model responses per photograph with a statement-by-statement mark-up, a short presentation comparing them with the documented history, and discussion notes.
acts.na: Students can compare two published descriptions of the same hoax photograph, one from its own era and one from a modern catalog, marking which statements are visible in the image.
acts.risk: Only public-domain photographs are entered. Class-written verbal descriptions of each image let blind and low-vision students take part in the mark-up.

acts.t: Reading aloud an AI team member's pre-generated interpretation of a public overdose chart in an interprofessional case
acts.sum: In an interprofessional course, graduate students in nursing, pharmacy, social work and related programs prepare a community case about opioid overdoses and then work through it in small groups led by faculty. While preparing the facilitator guide, faculty give an image-reading model a public-domain chart of overdose deaths over time from a federal surveillance report, along with the case materials, and ask it, in the role of a health services team member, what the chart shows and what the community should do. Faculty choose readings that will be instructive in discussion, for example one that attributes a change in the trend line to a policy without evidence of cause, one that misreads an axis or a footnote about provisional data, and one that is careful and accurate, and they keep these unedited in the guide. During the session the facilitator projects the chart and reads the agent's interpretation aloud at set points. Teams test each claim against the chart and its data notes, saying which are supported, which go beyond the data, and which are simply wrong, and then decide what, if anything, from the agent's reading they would carry into their plan for the community. Students never use the model themselves. The groups then come together to compare findings and how they split the checking of the agent's contributions across their professions.
acts.f: Arguing With and Against AI
acts.gate: Teams test each claim in the agent's reading against the chart and its data notes, then decide what, if anything, to carry into their plan.
acts.dl: Team annotations of each pre-generated claim (supported, beyond the data, wrong) and a section of the team's plan stating what it took from the agent's reading and why.
acts.na: The facilitator can read instructor-written interpretations of the chart that contain the same kinds of overreach, presented as a colleague's view.
acts.risk: Students do not use AI; faculty generate the readings in advance. A table of the chart's values accompanies the projection for screen-reader users.

acts.t: Having an image-reading model narrate a student's hand-drawn methods diagram, then checking the narration against the paper
acts.sum: Working from the methods section of an assigned study alone, students sketch its procedure by hand as a diagram, showing the variables the researchers changed, the outcomes they recorded, the sequence of steps, the units sampled and the number of repetitions, with each element tied to the research question it addresses. Instead of asking a tool to describe the paper, they photograph their own diagram and give only the photograph to an image-reading model, asking it to narrate step by step the experiment the diagram depicts. Because the model has not seen the paper, its narration tests what the drawing actually communicates. Students lay the narration beside the methods text and mark every departure: a step the narration adds, a sample size it invents, two conditions it merges, an order it reverses, a control it misses. For each departure they decide whether the diagram was ambiguous, quoting the methods sentence the diagram was meant to show, or whether the model misread a clear drawing, which they also record. They revise the diagram to remove the ambiguities they own and photograph it again for a second narration. Submissions include both diagrams, both narrations with departures marked, and a one-sentence statement of the design the paper used. A drawing whose elements cannot each be tied to a sentence of the methods counts as unfinished.

acts.t: Captioning paired public-domain portraits with an attention model and examining what each gendered word attended to
acts.sum: The instructor selects pairs of public-domain portraits of sitters of comparable standing, such as a woman and a man who were both scientists, rulers or writers of the same period, and checks that each pair offers a meaningful comparison and that the assigned scholarship covers both sitters. Students first read the scholarship and note how it establishes each sitter's context and achievement. The instructor then runs the portraits through the caption model built in the visual-attention tutorial, which writes a short caption and records, for every word, the region of the image it attended to. Students receive the captions and per-word attention maps rather than using the model themselves. They examine the language of each caption, which words name the sitter, describe appearance, or suggest action or status, and then check each gendered or status word against its attention map, asking whether the word rests on the person's face and body or on surrounding objects such as a book, a gown or a desk. They keep observations about these outputs separate from claims about the historical people, which come from the scholarship. Discussion moves through three levels, what attention-based captioning does in general, what this trained model took from its particular training images, and what follows from applying it to historical portraits, and considers whether the differences support a hypothesis about how those training images shape its descriptions and which further portrait pairs could challenge it. Students submit a short comparison quoting captions and attention evidence.
acts.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
acts.gate: Students compare captions for paired sitters and check whether gendered and status words rest on the person or on surrounding objects.
acts.dl: Captions and per-word attention maps for each portrait pair, a student comparison quoting both, and a stated hypothesis with the further pairs that would test it.
acts.na: Students can compare published museum catalog descriptions of the same portrait pairs, marking which words describe the person and which describe setting and dress.

acts.t: Coding public-domain documentary photographs, then weighing a multimodal model's descriptions against the image and the original caption
acts.sum: Students in a visual research methods course draw a sample of documentary photographs from a public-domain government collection of the 1930s and 1940s, each with the original caption written by the photographer or project staff. Working from a codebook the class agrees on, each student first codes every photograph, recording people, actions, setting, material conditions and any theme they see, and notes where the original caption steers the reading. A multimodal model is then asked for a detailed description of each photograph and a few theme tags, as in the digital humanities project the operation comes from, but it is given the image without its caption. Students break each description into claims and rate them: visible in the image, a reasonable inference, an inference the image cannot support, or plainly wrong, such as people miscounted or objects that are not there. They also compare the model's tags with their own codes and with the photographer's caption, which carries its own framing of poverty and dignity. Pairs compare their ratings on the same photographs and discuss where they disagree. Students submit the model's analysis together with their own assessment of it, and a short note on whether such descriptions would help or mislead someone searching the collection.

acts.gate: Students code first, then rate each description claim for accuracy and overreach and calibrate their ratings with a partner.
acts.dl: Student codes for each photograph, the model's descriptions and tags, a claim-by-claim rating sheet, pair calibration notes, and a short note on use in collection search.
acts.na: Students can rate one another's written descriptions of the same photographs with the same four categories and calibrate in pairs.
acts.risk: Only public-domain photographs are entered. Class-written descriptions let blind and low-vision students do the rating with a partner.

acts.t: Pairing a deep-research agent's report with a rerunnable database search for each claim
acts.sum: A researcher assembling the evidence behind an argument breaks it into questions that each pose a single proposition data could settle, and groups them under the parts of the argument they support. For each question, a deep-research agent is asked to plan the task before it runs; the researcher saves the plan, notes what it leaves out, such as a population, a time window, or a type of study, and edits the request where the plan is too broad. The agent then searches, reads, and produces a report with references, which is saved with its run date. Because a generated report cannot be rerun to the same result, the researcher builds a second, independent channel for each question: a field-tagged search strategy in a bibliographic database, written out in full so that anyone can repeat it, with its date and hit count. Reference sets from the two channels are deduplicated by identifier and compared. The researcher records the overlap, the references found only by the agent, and the references found only by the database, and reads a sample from each group to judge whether they bear on the claim. Questions on which the channels diverge sharply are flagged, the researcher checks whether the literature behind them is recent, unevenly indexed, or dominated by preprints, and the divergence is reported as a figure alongside the synthesis rather than smoothed over.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: The researcher critiques the agent's plan before it runs, compares its reference set with a written-out database search, and reports divergence between channels as a measurement.
acts.dl: For each claim, an annotated research plan, the dated agent report with references, a written database search strategy with date and hit count, an overlap table between channels, and a divergence figure reported with the synthesis.
acts.na: The researcher runs the database channel alone, with a second bibliographic database as the independent comparison.
acts.risk: Deep-research modes are often limited to paid tiers; the database channel needs library database access. Only the researcher's questions enter the tool.

acts.t: Catching a planted contraindication in a web-grounded answer and weighing the pages it cites
acts.sum: Occupational therapy doctoral students preparing for fieldwork watch their instructor put an instructor-written patient case to a web-grounded assistant during a seminar and ask it for intervention suggestions, so that the answer arrives with inline citations to the pages it drew on. The instructor selects three suggestions, one of them chosen deliberately because it is contraindicated for this patient, and saves each with its cited pages. Students do not use the tool themselves. In small groups they first examine the cited pages for each option: who published the page, what kind of evidence it reports, whether it addresses a population like this patient, and whether it actually supports the suggestion attached to it. They then search the professional literature themselves for each strategy, recording their database searches so they can be repeated. For each option the group states whether it would accept it, amend it, or reject it, with the grounds, and identifies what in the cited pages made the unsafe option look plausible. The instructor, who knows in advance which option is contraindicated and why, checks the groups' evidence reviews against that reasoning. In a follow-on individual assignment, students generate interventions for a new case on their own and document the evidence behind each.

acts.t: Fact-checking a generated biography and the provenance of the pages it cites
acts.sum: Students receive, or generate for the occasion, a short biography of a well-documented figure in their institution's history, written by a generative search engine with citations to web pages. Choosing someone with local records, such as archives, yearbooks, or news coverage, means the checking can be finished. Students first work through the biography with lateral reading in the SIFT pattern, stopping on each claim, investigating, finding better coverage, and tracing it to its origin, and they correct the errors they find. A second pass turns to the cited pages themselves. A recent audit of generative search engines, by its authors' account, found that a meaningful share of cited pages showed signs of being machine-written, so students examine each cited page's provenance by hand: whether an author or organization is named and can be found elsewhere, whether the page reports anything first-hand or only restates other pages, whether its dates and details agree with the archival record, and what the page seems designed to get readers to do. They do not run detection software, and they record a page as unestablished rather than machine-written when its origin cannot be determined. The product is a corrected biography with a source table that marks each cited page as reliable, secondary, or unestablished, and notes which errors in the biography trace to which pages.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Students fact-check each claim by lateral reading against local records, then examine each cited page's provenance, marking pages whose origin cannot be established as unestablished.
acts.dl: A corrected biography, a claim log with the evidence for each correction, and a source table classifying each cited page as reliable, secondary, or unestablished, linked to the errors it produced.
acts.na: Students fact-check a short web biography from an aggregator site with SIFT and assess the provenance of its sources in the same way.
acts.risk: Free-tier generative search engines suffice, and the instructor can supply a pre-generated biography. The subject should be a figure in the institution's public history, not a private individual.
