acts.gate: Students produce a confidence-rated recall of which court hears each case, and each group marks every label, level, and appeal path on the chart as correct, wrong, or unverifiable, with corrections drawn from the published court charts.
acts.dl: A group-annotated copy of the AI-generated court chart with each label, level and appeal path marked and corrected, plus each student's confidence-rated recall sheet.
acts.risk: Students need no device, account or payment; the chart is distributed on paper with a text description of its levels and paths available for students who use screen readers.

acts.t: Rehearsing a Family Conference on Classroom Behavior Expectations
acts.sum: Teacher candidates in an early childhood methods course rehearse a family conference with a conversational AI playing a parent, after drafting classroom rules and a behavior support plan for a child in an instructor-written vignette. The vignette and the candidate's own plan are the only material given to the tool; the IRIS case study unit on early childhood behavior management is read as published on the IRIS site, and its strategy sheets serve as the reference candidates consult. In the role-play the simulated parent asks why a rule is worded as it is, questions whether it fits the family's routines at home, and may resist parts of the plan. The candidate explains, adjusts, or holds a position. Afterward, candidates annotate the transcript, tying each thing they said to a strategy in the published sheets or marking it as unsupported, and they revise the plan. A debrief with the instructor or a cooperating teacher takes up what a text exchange leaves out of a live conference with a family.
acts.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
acts.gate: Teacher candidates draft the rules and support plan, explain or adjust them under the simulated parent's questions, tie each thing they said to a published strategy or mark it unsupported, and revise the plan.
acts.dl: An annotated role-play transcript and a revised set of classroom rules and behavior support plan for the vignette child.
acts.risk: The vignette is fictional and instructor-written, so no information about real children or families is entered; candidates who prefer not to use the tool can rehearse with a peer playing the parent.

acts.t: Sorting AI-Suggested Supports into Accommodations and Modifications
acts.sum: Candidates in a special education or inclusive-practice course ask a conversational AI for 'accommodations' for a student described in an instructor-written profile, then sort what comes back. The published IRIS use-case idea on accommodations versus modifications is completed first, as it stands on the IRIS site, and none of its scenarios are entered into the tool. The profile is fictional, for example a seventh grader with a specific learning disability in written expression in a general education science class. The tool often returns a mixed list under the single heading it was asked for: extended time and speech-to-text beside shortened assignments or a simplified text. Candidates label each suggestion as an accommodation or a modification, justify the call in a sentence, and mark each as accepted, amended, or declined for this student. They also record any suggestion that would need information the profile does not contain. The sorted list is checked against the definitions in the published overview and the course's reference on individualized education programs.

acts.gate: Candidates label each suggestion as an accommodation or a modification with a one-sentence justification, mark it accepted, amended or declined for this student, and record any suggestion that needs information the profile lacks.
acts.dl: A sorted and annotated list of the tool's suggestions, each classified, justified, and marked accepted, amended or declined for the profiled student.
acts.risk: The student profile is fictional and instructor-written, so no information about a real student's disability or services is entered into a tool.

acts.t: Auditing a Delegated Evidence Search for a Named Practice
acts.sum: A teacher-education faculty member preparing an evidence review on a named instructional program delegates a bounded search to an agentic research tool and then audits each step of what it did. Before delegating, the faculty member writes down their initial thoughts: which studies they expect to find, for which grade levels and student populations, and what would count as a match for the setting they are writing about. The agent is given the program name and those inclusion criteria, searches across sites, and returns a report with citations and a log of its steps. The audit works through the log. Each citation is resolved in ERIC or at the publisher; each study's sample, grade band, and setting are read in the methods section and compared with what the report says; any What Works Clearinghouse intervention report is checked for its rating and the population it covers. Studies the agent omitted are added from a database search. The initial thoughts are then revisited against the audited set. The IRIS module on fidelity of implementation supplies the topic only.

acts.dl: An audited evidence table for the named program, listing each study with its verified sample, grade band and setting, alongside the faculty member's initial and revised expectations.

acts.t: Spoken and Typed Explanations of Fraction Equivalence, Compared
acts.sum: Candidates in an elementary mathematics methods course explain why three-fourths and six-eighths name the same amount twice, once by speaking to a speech-to-text tool and once by typing, and compare what each medium kept. The task is specified by its objective only: an accurate explanation, pitched at fourth graders, that refers to a representation such as a number line or fraction strips. The speech tool returns a transcript, which may render spoken fractions, 'numerator', or 'equal parts' incorrectly and which carries the pauses and restarts of talk. Candidates correct the transcript against their own recording, then set the spoken and typed versions side by side and score both with the same criteria. They note which version states the multiplicative relationship more clearly, which leans on the representation, and what the transcript lost that the voice carried. A short written comparison addresses whether written prose is essential to this objective or one of several acceptable media, the question raised by the CAST consideration on multiple media for communication.

acts.gate: Each candidate explains the equivalence aloud and in typing, corrects the transcript against their own recording, scores both versions on the same criteria, and writes whether written prose is essential to the objective.
acts.dl: A corrected transcript, a typed explanation, both scored on the same criteria, and a short written comparison of the two media.

acts.t: Marking Meaning Shifts in AI Simplifications of Methods Prose
acts.sum: Graduate students in an education research methods course receive AI-written plain-language versions of a dense methods passage and mark where the simplification changed what a technical term means. The instructor prepares the materials ahead of time by giving a conversational AI tool a paragraph from an openly licensed article, one reporting score reliability, a confidence interval, and a statistically significant difference with a small effect size, and saving two or three of its rewrites. In class, students first write their own gloss of each term from the original paragraph, unaided. They then read the rewrites beside the original and annotate each place where clearer syntax came with a changed claim: 'significant' read as important, 'reliable' as accurate, an interval described as the range of most students' scores. For each mark, the student writes the corrected plain-language sentence. Annotations are checked against the original passage and the definitions in the course's measurement reference. Students use no AI tool; the rewrites are specimens.

acts.gate: Each student writes an unaided gloss of each term, marks every place a rewrite changed what a technical term means, and writes a corrected plain-language sentence for each mark.
acts.dl: An annotated set of AI rewrites with each meaning shift marked and a corrected plain-language sentence written for it, alongside the student's own unaided glosses.
acts.risk: Students need no device, account or payment, and because the passage is openly licensed it can be distributed in accessible formats along with the rewrites.

acts.t: Reviewing a Lesson-Plan Comment Bank in a Hosted Assistant
acts.sum: A methods instructor reviews the bank of reusable comments they attach to lesson-plan submissions, using an institutionally hosted assistant to sort the comments and draft alternatives. Only the instructor's own comment bank and the assignment rubric are loaded; no student work or names enter the system. The assistant labels each comment as one that only judges ('objective unclear', 'strong hook') or one that names a next action, and for the first kind it drafts a version pointing to something the candidate could do, such as rewriting the objective with an observable verb and a condition. The instructor has already sorted a sample of the comments by hand, and compares that sort with the assistant's before reading the drafts. Each draft is then accepted, amended, or rejected, with a brief reason, and checked against the rubric row it refers to so that the rewritten comment still describes the criterion. The CAST consideration on action-oriented feedback is read as published as the lens for the sort. The result is a revised bank and a record of the instructor's decisions.

acts.dl: A revised comment bank for the lesson-plan assignment, with a log of which assistant drafts the instructor accepted, amended or rejected and why.

acts.t: Sparring with a Chatbot Before a Camera-Policy Case Discussion
acts.sum: Before a seminar discussion of the Justice in Schools case 'Remote Control', which students read as published, each student argues with a conversational AI about a general question the case raises: whether a school may require young children to keep cameras on during online class at home. The student writes a position in their own words and asks the tool to act as an opponent for several rounds; the case text is not pasted in. The tool tends to supply ready arguments about oversight, consistency, privacy, and equity. Students then read their transcript with a set of questions: whose voice is heard in these arguments, whose is missing, who decides, and at whose cost. They list the objections that changed their position, the ones they rejected and why, and the people in the case, such as particular families or the teachers on the team, whose situation the exchange never reached. The seminar itself runs without AI, and each student defends a decision for the fourth-grade team.

acts.gate: The student writes a position in their own words, lists the objections that changed it and those rejected with reasons, names the people the exchange never reached, and defends a decision in a seminar run without AI.
acts.dl: A sparring transcript annotated for heard and missing voices, a list of objections accepted and rejected, and an oral defense of a decision in seminar.
acts.risk: Students enter only their own position statement and no case text; a student who does not use the tool can annotate a transcript the instructor supplies, and the seminar itself requires no technology.

acts.t: Checking an AI-Drafted Teacher Evaluation Against the Rubric
acts.sum: Students in an educational leadership course examine a teacher evaluation narrative drafted by a document-grounded assistant and decide whether they would sign it. Pairs give the assistant two documents: a publicly available teacher-evaluation rubric and a set of instructor-written observation notes on a fictional middle school science teacher whose lab routines run smoothly and whose questioning rarely goes beyond recall. It drafts a rating for each rubric domain with a supporting paragraph. Students trace every sentence of the draft to a line in the notes and a level descriptor in the rubric, marking evidence the draft weighed, evidence it passed over, and claims found in neither document. They assign their own ratings and write a short justification of each difference from the draft. The Justice in Schools case 'First Rate', read as published and not entered into the tool, then frames discussion of what a rating sets in motion and what remains the evaluator's responsibility when a draft arrives already written.

acts.gate: Pairs produce a trace of every sentence of the draft to the observation notes and rubric, their own rating for each domain, and a written justification of each difference from the draft.
acts.dl: A marked-up evaluation draft with each sentence traced to the notes and rubric, the pair's own domain ratings, and a written justification of each difference.
acts.risk: The observation notes describe a fictional teacher, so no personnel information about a real educator is entered; the rubric used is one that is publicly available.

acts.t: Locating and Verifying Statutory Guidance Behind a School Decision
acts.sum: Students studying the Justice in Schools case 'No Laughing Matter', read as published, use an AI search tool to locate the statutory guidance on the Prevent duty for schools in England and verify what the tool says the guidance requires. The query is the student's own; the case text is not entered. The tool returns a summary with links and may paraphrase loosely, cite superseded versions, or attribute requirements to the guidance that are not found in it. Students open the current official publication, find each passage the summary relies on, and record the paragraph number, the exact wording, and whether the summary's paraphrase holds. They note the date and version of the document they are reading. With the verified passages in hand, each student writes a brief analysis of whether the head teacher's stated justification in the case is supported by, in tension with, or outside the scope of the guidance. Seminar discussion of the case's wider questions about expression and inclusion proceeds from the verified text.

acts.t: Comparing a Model's Weld Defect Calls with Instructor Inspection
acts.sum: Learners in a first-year welding lab photograph their own practice welds and compare a multimodal model's reading of each photograph with the instructor's visual inspection. After completing a fillet or groove weld coupon, the learner first inspects it and records what they see: undercut, porosity, overlap, incomplete fusion, or an acceptable profile. The model is then given the photograph and asked what discontinuities are visible. It may name a defect that is not present, miss one that lighting or angle obscures, or describe the bead in general terms. The instructor inspects the physical coupon against the visual acceptance criteria the program uses and completes the assessment sheet. Learners tabulate the three readings for each coupon, their own, the model's, and the instructor's, and note where a photograph could not show what a gauge or a change of viewing angle revealed. The SkillsCommons record for WELD 154 supplies the occupational setting; no course documents from it are uploaded.

acts.gate: The learner records their own inspection of each coupon before the model sees it, tabulates it beside the model's and the instructor's readings, and notes what the photograph could not show that a gauge or another viewing angle revealed.
acts.dl: A table for each practice coupon comparing the learner's inspection, the model's defect call and the instructor's assessment, with notes on what the photograph could not show.
acts.risk: A camera phone and a multimodal tool are needed; a shared lab device and instructor-run session avoid requiring personal accounts, and photographs show only the coupon, not people or the shop.

acts.t: Correcting an Agent-Compiled Timeline After an Interprofessional Simulation
acts.sum: After a simulation day in which several health and public-safety programs work one instructor-written scenario in sequence, learners correct an incident timeline that an agentic AI system compiled from their notes. Each program submits its own documentation: a rescue run report, a nursing handoff note, a laboratory requisition, an officer's scene notes. Under instructor supervision, the agent collects the submissions, orders the events, reconciles times, and produces a single timeline with a log of what it took from which note. In the debrief, mixed-program groups read the timeline against the facilitator's event log and the session recording. They mark events placed out of order, handoffs the timeline merged or dropped, and entries where the agent resolved a conflict between two notes without saying so. Each program then identifies which of the errors began in its own documentation and which in the compilation. The simulation uses no real patient information. The idea of a single scenario passing through many occupational programs comes from the LATI Healthcare Mega Simulation record.
acts.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
acts.gate: Mixed-program groups mark events out of order, handoffs merged or dropped, and conflicts resolved without notice, checked against the event log and recording, and each program identifies which errors began in its own documentation.
acts.dl: A corrected incident timeline annotated by mixed-program groups, with each error attributed to a program's documentation or to the compilation.
acts.risk: Learner-written notes are processed by the agent, so an institutionally approved tool and learner notice are relevant; the scenario is fictional and contains no real patient information, and recordings are handled under the programs' existing simulation consent practices.

acts.t: Autocomplete and AI Search Answers Compared for Representation
acts.sum: Pairs in a first-year library session put the same identity and occupation query stems to two systems, a conventional search engine's autocomplete and an AI search assistant, and log what each returns. The session keeps the sequence of the Project CORA lesson it adapts: the librarian models a search on screen, pairs work through a worksheet, and a think-pair-share closes the half hour. The worksheet here has two columns. In one, pairs copy the completions the search engine offers for each stem; in the other, they record the assistant's answer to the completed question and the sources it links. Pairs then label each entry as informing, steering, or narrowing: whether the system leaves several options in view, pushes toward one, or delivers a single synthesized account. Discussion turns on which groups are described differently in the two columns and on where each description appears to come from. A statement about a group in the assistant's answer is opened at its linked source and read there before the pair records it as supported.
acts.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
acts.gate: Pairs produce a two-column log with each entry labeled informing, steering or narrowing, read each statement about a group at its linked source before recording it as supported, and give a spoken account of one difference in representation.
acts.dl: A completed two-column evidence log with each entry classified and a short spoken account of one difference in how a group is represented.
acts.risk: Query stems are written by the librarian and pairs share one device, so no student needs a personal account; some completions may be offensive, and the stems can be screened beforehand.

acts.t: Mapping Chatbot Data Flows Without Entering Personal Information
acts.sum: Participants in a library workshop on generative AI and privacy work from a printed packet and type nothing into any tool. The packet holds the public privacy notices and terms of use of two conversational AI services, reached by link, and three sample exchanges the librarian produced beforehand from invented prompts containing no personal details. Small groups read the terms closely and mark what the service says it retains, who else receives it, how long it is kept, and whether prompts are used for training. Each data flow they find is then placed on the Agent-Impact Matrix for Artificial Intelligence used in the published Hidden Layer workshop, so that the group names who acts and who is affected. The sample exchanges give the groups something concrete to trace: for a given prompt, which clauses apply to it. The session rests on a distinction between using a tool fluently and knowing how it is funded and governed. A placement on the matrix stands only when the group can point to the clause in the notice that supports it.
acts.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
acts.gate: Each group produces a matrix of the data flows it found in the terms, naming who acts and who is affected, with every placement tied to the clause of the privacy notice or terms that supports it.
acts.dl: A completed matrix of data flows for one service, each entry annotated with the clause of the privacy notice or terms it rests on.
acts.risk: No account, device, or personal information is required of participants; privacy notices are long legal texts, so excerpts with plain-language glosses and accessible digital copies support participants who use screen readers.

acts.t: Three-Way Reference Check on Grounded and Ungrounded AI Lists
acts.sum: Students request five references on an instructor-assigned topic from two tools, a source-grounded assistant that retrieves from indexed literature and a general chat model working without retrieval, and then try to find every item. The check is the one set out in the published 5-Minute Reference Check: each reference is looked up by resolving its DOI at doi.org or by searching the exact title in a scholarly search engine or library discovery, and is classified as found-and-matches, found-but-differs, or not-found. Items that are not found are retried before a conclusion is drawn, and entries that differ are corrected from the actual record. Tallies for the two lists go on a shared board. Because output from generative systems may include references that are well formed and point to no existing work, the lists are treated as claims to be tested, not as bibliographies. Students then revise one prompt, for instance by asking for DOIs, rerun it, and note whether the tally changes. Every classification is recorded with the lookup that produced it.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Students look up every reference, classify each as found and matching, found but differing, or not found with the lookup that settled it, correct entries that differ, and note whether a revised prompt changed the tally.
acts.dl: A classification table for ten references with the lookup evidence for each, the two tallies, and a note on what the revised prompt changed.
acts.risk: The topic prompt is supplied by the instructor, so no student writing enters a tool; source-grounded assistants are often subscription products, and a shared class or library login avoids individual cost.

acts.t: Scholarly Party Guest Lists by Citation Chaining and AI Search
acts.sum: Groups plan a 'scholarly party' around one starting article and then compare their guest list with one an AI research assistant builds from the same article. As in the published Scholarly Party use-case idea, each group evaluates its article, sets a party theme that serves as an early research question, uses citation tracking to decide which scholars to invite, and looks for gaps: disciplines or viewpoints missing from the list. Here the group also gives the assistant the article's citation and the theme and asks who belongs in the conversation. The two lists are set side by side. For each invitee the assistant proposes, the group looks the scholar and work up in a library database and records whether the work exists, whether it cites or is cited by the starting article, or whether the connection cannot be traced. Invitees found by only one method are discussed in the facilitator-led debrief, where the assistant's list is treated as one more contribution open to challenge, alongside each group's own reading of who is missing.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: The group builds its own guest list by citation tracking, records for each invitee the assistant proposed whether the work exists and connects to the starting article, and names the disciplines or viewpoints missing.
acts.dl: An annotated guest list showing which invitees came from citation tracking, which from the assistant, the verification result for each, and the gaps the group identified.
acts.risk: Only the article's citation and the group's theme are entered, not the article text; AI research assistants vary in free-tier limits, so one shared account per group keeps cost and sign-up to a minimum.

acts.t: Staff Workshop on Chat-Proposed Author Name Merges
acts.sum: Metadata and repository staff meet for a working session on a recurring chore, reconciling variant author names, and compare two ways of proposing merges before deciding how either fits the unit's routine. The session uses the Library Carpentry OpenRefine lesson's sample of article metadata. Staff split the multi-valued author column, run Cluster and Edit with the key-collision fingerprint method, and note the clusters it forms. The list of distinct name forms from the same column then goes to a chat model with a request for proposed merges and a reason for each. Working in pairs, staff log every proposal from either method as accepted, amended, or rejected, with the grounds for the decision; names that may belong to different people are set aside for a human lookup. The session treats the two methods and the staff as a division of labor, in which the tools surface candidates and the decision and its record stay with the cataloger. Discussion closes on which categories of merge the unit would hand to either method.

acts.gate: Staff decide whether each proposed merge is accepted, amended, or rejected and record the grounds, set aside names that may belong to different people for a human lookup, and decide which categories of merge the unit would hand to either method.
acts.dl: A merge log listing each proposed cluster, its origin, the decision taken, and the grounds, plus a short list of cases reserved for human lookup.

acts.t: Annotating Archival Photographs Before a Vision Model Describes Them
acts.sum: Students in a library, archives, or museum studies course each annotate the same small set of public-domain photographs from a digital collection, compare their labels with peers, and only then see how a vision-language model describes the same images. The order follows the bias episode of the Intro to AI for GLAM course, where learners label images independently, compare, and afterwards view a classifier's predictions; here a model's free-text descriptions take the classifier's place. Students submit each photograph with a neutral request for a description and place the output beside their own and their peers' annotations. They mark which cultural details the model names, which it omits, and which it renders in generic or English-default terms, such as a specific garment or ceremony reduced to a broad category. Two questions organize the written comparison: whose way of seeing the image is reflected in each description, and who decided. The holding institution's catalog record, withheld until this point, is then opened, and all three sets of labels are read against it.

acts.gate: Students produce their own annotations of each photograph before seeing the model's, and a written comparison of whose way of seeing each description reflects, read against the holding institution's catalog record.
acts.dl: A comparison table for each photograph setting the student's, peers', and model's descriptions beside the catalog record, with a short written analysis of omissions and default terms.
acts.risk: Photographs are chosen from public-domain or openly licensed collections so that upload is permitted, and images of identifiable living people or culturally restricted material are left out; a shared account avoids individual sign-up.

acts.t: Drafting and Correcting SPARQL for a Wikidata Research Query
acts.sum: A researcher assembling a dataset from Wikidata, for example the publishers and places of publication of a set of nineteenth-century periodicals, has a coding assistant draft the SPARQL and then corrects it against the live knowledge graph. Before requesting anything, the researcher writes the question in plain language, sketches the columns expected, and lists a handful of items already known to belong in the result. The assistant's draft is run in the Wikidata Query Service. Property and item identifiers in the query are a frequent point of error, since a model may supply an identifier that exists but refers to something else, so each one is opened on its Wikidata page and its label read. The known items serve as a test: when one is absent from the results, the query or the underlying data is at fault, and a maintenance-style query for items missing the relevant statement shows which. The approach follows the Library Carpentry Wikidata lesson's move from a first single-item query to maintenance queries. Corrections are kept in a dated query log alongside each version.

acts.t: Decoding AI Descriptions Written for Two National Audiences
acts.sum: Students ask a chat model to describe one current international issue for news audiences in two different countries and then analyze the two texts as media documents. The exercise follows a lesson from Project Look Sharp's Global Media Perspectives kit, taught as published and reached by link, in which students compare coverage of an issue across countries of production. None of the kit's documents or questions is entered into the model; the issue and the analysis questions are written by the instructor. Students record what each output foregrounds, whose position is given first, which terms are used for the parties, and what is left out. Where the class has the languages, the request is repeated in a second language, and the same prompt is run on a second system, so that differences attributable to language or to developer can be seen. The discussion asks whether the model's 'local' version reflects that country's own reporting or an outside, often English-language, picture of it. Factual statements in each output are checked against reporting by news organizations based in the country named.

acts.gate: Students record what each output foregrounds, whose position comes first, which terms name the parties and what is left out, and mark each factual statement as confirmed or not by reporting from news organizations in the country named.
acts.dl: A side-by-side decoding of two AI-written descriptions, with framing differences annotated and each factual statement marked as confirmed or not confirmed by in-country reporting.
acts.risk: Prompts are instructor-written and no kit material is uploaded; the kit's lesson files require a free login on the publisher's site, and multilingual students may be asked to translate only if they volunteer.

acts.t: Interviewing an AI Stakeholder Before a Water Rights Role-Play
acts.sum: In a unit on water and agriculture, each student group interviews a chat model that has been directed to speak as one party to a water-allocation dispute, such as an irrigation district manager, a municipal utility planner, or a bottling company representative. The interviews prepare the class for the perspectives role-play in Project Look Sharp's kit Media Constructions of Sustainability: Food, Water, and Agriculture, which is then taught as published, by link. The persona briefs given to the model are written by the instructor from public records, and no kit reading or handout is entered into the tool. Groups ask what the party wants, what it fears, and what evidence it relies on, and from the transcript they draw a stakeholder map of priorities and points of conflict. A persona's answers are treated as claims about a position, not as the voice of the people represented. Before the role-play, each group checks three statements from its transcript against the party's own published documents, such as agency reports, utility plans, or company filings, and corrects its map.

acts.t: Auditing Age in AI Images of Creative Work
acts.sum: Students run a fixed set of prompts through an image generator, naming creative and helping occupations such as musician, music teacher, woodworker, and home health aide without stating an age, and count who appears. The audit accompanies Project Look Sharp's kit Creativity & Aging Through the Lens of Film, whose film-clip lessons are taught as published, by link, and from which nothing is entered into the generator. Each prompt is generated a set number of times, and pairs tally the apparent age group and gender of the figures using a codebook the class writes. A second round adds 'older' to each prompt, and students code how the generator then signals age: setting, posture, props, level of movement, and whether the figure is shown making something or being helped. The analysis traces the patterns to what such systems learn from existing images and asks whether the outputs repeat or depart from the portrayals studied in the film lessons. Pairs exchange image sets and recode a sample to test the codebook. The age tallies are set against published labor-force figures for the occupations named.

acts.t: Research Quest with an AI Informant of Mixed Reliability
acts.sum: Small groups play a cooperative research game in which a chatbot, set up by the instructor, speaks as an informant character whose leads cannot be taken on trust. The scenario, written by the instructor for the course, gives each party of three to five a question to answer and an argument to assemble, such as whether a town's vanished industry closed for the reason local memory gives. The informant offers leads in character: a title, an author, a claimed finding, a place to look. Some leads correspond to real sources in the library's holdings and some may not, because the model often produces plausible references that do not exist. A lead counts toward the party's progress only after a member has located the source in the catalog or a database and read enough to confirm the claim attached to it. Roles rotate each session, so that the player questioning the informant, the player searching and the player keeping the evidence record change. The party's closing argument cites only confirmed sources.

acts.gate: The party produces an evidence record of each lead, where it was or was not located, and why it was trusted or set aside, and a jointly written argument citing only sources members confirmed.

acts.risk: One shared device per party is enough, so individual accounts are not required; the scenario text given to the chatbot is instructor-written and nothing from the published game is entered into a tool.

acts.t: Four Moves Applied to One AI Search Answer
acts.sum: First-year students take a single answer from an AI search tool and work through it with the four SIFT moves, keeping a record of every correction. Each student poses one factual question tied to the course, such as whether a city's lead-pipe replacement program reduced measured lead levels, and saves the answer with its citations. The Stop move is a written note of what the student already knows about the question and what the answer is for. For Investigate, each cited source is looked up to learn who is behind it. For Find, the student sets the answer aside and looks for reporting or expert consensus on the central claim. For Trace, one quotation or statistic in the answer is followed to its original context. The correction log has a line for each sentence of the answer: confirmed, corrected, or not supported by any source found, with the source that settled it. Students finish by rewriting the answer in their own words from the sources they verified.

acts.gate: The student produces a sentence-by-sentence correction log naming the source that settled each line, and a rewritten answer in their own words drawn from the sources they verified.
acts.dl: A sentence-by-sentence correction log for one AI search answer, with the settling source for each line, and a rewritten answer based on verified sources.
acts.risk: Several AI search tools answer a limited number of questions without an account; students enter only a question, and those who prefer not to use a tool can work from an answer the instructor has saved.

acts.t: Checking an AI Profile of an Outside Organization
acts.sum: A committee that reviews outside organizations, such as groups offering free curriculum materials, guest speakers or sponsored research summaries, adds a short paired check to its intake routine. For each organization, one member asks an AI search tool who is behind it, who funds it and what it advocates, and saves the answer with its citations. A second member, without seeing that answer, carries out the quick independent lookup described in Mike Caulfield's post on investigating a source, which members read as published by link, and then glances at the references of the encyclopedia article that lookup leads to. The two accounts are compared on three points: funding, affiliations, and stated purpose. The committee notes where the AI answer repeats the organization's self-description, which often happens when the organization's own site is the main source the tool retrieved, and where it cites anything independent. Disagreements between the two accounts are resolved by going to the cited documents, and the outcome is filed with the committee's record for that organization.

acts.t: What the Article Implies but Never States
acts.sum: Journalism students use a document-grounded assistant to surface what a news article implies without saying, then test those implications against wider coverage. The instructor chooses an openly licensed or public-domain article on a contested local event, one in which the individual statements are checkable. Before using the tool, each student writes two sentences on how the article left them feeling about the event and what they think it wants a reader to conclude. The article is then loaded into the assistant, which is asked to list conclusions a reader would likely draw that the text never states, and to quote the passages that invite each one. Students check every quoted passage against the article, since the assistant may paraphrase and present it as quotation. They then look for other reporting and expert accounts of the same event and ask of each implication: is it supported there, contradicted, or left open? A final seminar turns on whose voices and what context the article's arrangement left out.

acts.t: Whom a Chatbot Names as an Authority
acts.sum: After completing a self-paced lesson on authority as constructed and contextual, students ask a chatbot who the authorities are on a topic from their course and examine the pattern in its answer. Groups take one topic, such as groundwater management or postpartum care, and pose the question several ways: for a general reader, for practitioners in a named region, for the community most affected, and, where a group member can, in a second language. Each response is saved. The names and bodies returned are tallied by type: university researchers, government agencies, professional associations, practitioners, community organizations. Groups look up a sample of the named people to confirm that they exist and hold the roles described. The discussion compares the tallies across the versions of the question, asking which kinds of authority the chatbot returns by default, which appear only when a context is specified, and who is named by a subject librarian or a course reading and absent from every response.

acts.gate: The group produces a tally of the authorities named under each version of the question and an account of which kinds appeared by default, which only with a context, and who was absent from every response.
acts.dl: A tally sheet of the authorities named under each version of the question, with a group account of which kinds appeared by default and which were absent.
acts.risk: A free chatbot tier is sufficient and one device per group reduces account requirements; the lesson is assigned by link as published on the project's site, where some external components may no longer work.

acts.t: Evidence Types in an AI Assistant's Clinical Answer
acts.sum: Students in clinical programs put an instructor-written clinical question to an AI research assistant and judge whether the kinds of studies it returns suit the kind of question asked. Questions differ by type across the class: a therapy question such as whether chlorhexidine bathing reduces central-line infections in adult intensive care, a prognosis question, a question about patients' experience of a treatment. Before searching, each student states which research designs would best answer their question. The assistant's answer and its cited studies are saved. The student then opens each cited study and classifies it from its methods section: systematic review, randomized trial, cohort study, qualitative study, guideline, or something else. Three things are recorded for each: whether the study exists as cited, whether the assistant's description of its design is accurate, and whether that design fits the question type. Each returned study is accepted, replaced or rejected with a reason, and gaps are filled from a database search using the appropriate study-type filter.

acts.t: Campus-Licensed and Free AI Tools: What Each Can Reach
acts.sum: A library working group compares what a campus-licensed AI tool and a free consumer one can reach when asked the same course-related questions, and records who pays for each route to the information. Members draft ten questions drawn from actual course guides across disciplines. Each question is put to both tools, and the sources each answer cites are sorted into four groups: openly available, behind a paywall the library subscribes to, behind a paywall it does not, and not locatable. For each tool the group also notes the terms that apply: who holds the license, what the institution pays, and what the provider's data terms say about retention of what users enter. The same questions are then run in the library's discovery search to see what the collection provides that neither tool surfaced. The findings are written up under three headings, teaching implications, governance and day-to-day operations, as a short briefing for the committee that advises on campus AI tool provision.

acts.t: Tracing a Coding Assistant's Drawing Rules to the Diagram
acts.sum: Studio students diagram the logic of a precedent drawn from self-assembly or nano-scale systems and, before opening any tool, write down the rules they expect a drawing generator to need. Each student then describes the diagram in plain language to a coding assistant, which returns a candidate Processing sketch. The sketch is run, and the student annotates its code line by line against the logic diagram, marking which generated rules correspond to a relation in the diagram, which were added by the assistant without any basis in the precedent, and which diagrammed relations are missing. Students record their own judgment of the sketch before asking the assistant to explain its choices, and note where the explanation and the code disagree. The assistant's sketch is then set aside and the student writes the generator, keeping only rules that can be traced to the diagram. At the pin-up, the diagram, the annotated candidate and the student-authored drawings hang side by side, so that every mark in the final drawing can be followed back to a stated rule.

acts.t: Plaster Forecasts Checked Against the Sectioned Cast
acts.sum: Students design a spatial construct that works as formwork, cast plaster in the voids it defines, and cut sections through the result. Before pouring, each student describes the formwork in writing to a conversational assistant, giving dimensions, orientation, pour point and mix, and asks where the plaster will fill completely, where air may be trapped, and where the cast is likely to break on release. The forecast is printed and pinned beside the formwork. After the cast is sectioned, students mark each prediction on the cut face as confirmed, partly confirmed or contradicted, and add what the section shows that no forecast mentioned, such as settling lines, surface texture taken from the formwork, or voids the description never implied. A short written comparison separates errors that came from the student's own incomplete description from those that came from the assistant's general account of plaster. The physical section is treated as the evidence throughout, and the forecast as a claim to be tested against it.

acts.t: AI-Written Wall Labels Checked Against Appropriation Art
acts.sum: Students receive three short wall labels that the instructor produced beforehand with a conversational AI tool, prompted only with each work's artist, title and date. The works are chosen from the exemplar set on a museum's published reference page for the term appropriation, which students open by link and read as published; no museum text or image is entered into the tool. Working in pairs and using no AI themselves, students test every sentence of each label. For each claim about what the artist borrowed, from where, and how it was altered, they look at the reproduction on the museum's object page, read the object record, and mark the claim as visible in the work, stated in the record, or not found in either. They also ask whether the label describes an intentional alteration, as the page's definition of the term requires, or only notes a resemblance. Each pair rewrites one label so that every sentence can be pointed to in the object or its record, and the class compares which kinds of claims most often lacked support.

acts.t: Correcting a Machine Transcript of an Oral History Interview
acts.sum: Each student records an interview with an elder or other person they admire, following a national oral history program's published guidance and tools, which are used as provided by link. With the narrator's stated consent to this further step, the student runs the recording through a speech-to-text tool and receives a first-pass transcript. The student then listens to the full recording with the transcript in hand and corrects it. Every correction is entered in an error catalog under a category: names of people and places, dialect or regional vocabulary, overlapping speech, and non-verbal sound such as pauses, laughter or a change in voice that carried meaning the tool did not register. For three passages, the student writes a sentence on how the uncorrected transcript would have changed what the narrator appears to say. The corrected transcript goes back to the narrator for review before anything is deposited or shared, and the catalog is discussed in class as evidence of what a transcript, machine-made or human-made, leaves out of a spoken account.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Students produce the consented interview, a transcript corrected against their own recording, a categorized error catalog, and three notes on how the uncorrected transcript would have changed what the narrator appears to say.
acts.dl: A corrected interview transcript reviewed by the narrator, with a categorized catalog of transcription errors and three short interpretive notes.
acts.risk: A narrator's voice and personal account are sensitive data, so the design depends on explicit consent for transcription and on a tool that does not retain audio; captioned playback or an alternative role is needed for students who are deaf or hard of hearing.

acts.t: Illustrating Testimony: Generated Panels Checked Against the Interview
acts.sum: Journalism students interview a person about an event that person witnessed, with consent, and script a one-page comic from the interview in which every panel description is tied to a quoted or paraphrased line in their notes. The idea of treating a comic built from firsthand accounts as a primary source comes from a published news lesson on comics journalism, which can be read separately by link; none of its excerpts are used here. For two panels, an image generator produces an illustration from the student's panel description, with the interviewee's name and identifying details removed. The student also makes the same panels by hand, in whatever medium the course uses. Each generated panel is then audited against the interview notes. Students list every depicted detail, such as weather, damage, clothing, bystanders and facial expression, and mark whether the interviewee said it, implied it, or never mentioned it. They ask the same question of their own hand-made panel. A short editor's note states which version, if either, could be published as an account of what the interviewee reported, and why.

acts.gate: Students produce the interview, a comic script tying each panel to their notes, hand-made panels, a detail audit, and an editor's note on which version could stand as an account of what the interviewee reported.

acts.t: Sourcing National Debt Campaign Claims with a Grounded Assistant
acts.sum: Groups design a public awareness campaign about the US national debt, working from a published news lesson's campaign brief used as provided by link. Before any slogan or fact card is written, each group lists the questions its campaign needs answered: how large the debt is, what it is composed of, who holds it, and what it costs to service. The group looks up each answer directly in official federal publications and records the table and date. It then puts the same questions to a document-grounded assistant loaded only with those public-domain federal documents; the lesson's video and text are not placed in the tool. For every figure the assistant returns, the group opens the passage it cites and records whether the number, unit, date and definition match, for example whether a total refers to debt held by the public or to gross debt. Mismatches are logged and corrected. Campaign materials carry a source line for every figure, and during peer critique another group picks three claims at random and traces them to the table.

acts.t: Arguing a Standards Decision Against a Rival Producer Persona
acts.sum: Students read a published journalism ethics case about a network standards editor's deadline decision on airing photographs, obtained from the publisher as provided, and each settles on a ruling before class. A conversational assistant is then set up with a short instructor-written persona: a producer at a competing network who argues that the pictures are already public, that audiences expect them, and that holding back concedes the story. The persona brief is the instructor's own; no case text is pasted into the tool, and students argue in their own words. Each student defends the ruling through several exchanges while the persona presses on competition and time. Afterward, students annotate the transcript. They mark which of their arguments rested on a written standards policy or a documented fact in the case, which rested on assertion, and where the persona made a claim about the events that the case does not contain. A no-AI seminar follows in which students compare annotated transcripts and state whether the pressure changed their ruling or only their reasons.

acts.t: Tracing AI Search Results on Community Newspaper Business Models
acts.sum: A faculty member preparing a study of how community newspapers have managed the move to digital revenue uses an AI research-search tool for the scoping stage of the literature review. The question comes from a published 2014 teaching case about a family-owned paper weighing whether to make several linked changes at once or in phases; the case is read as published and none of it is entered into the tool. The researcher writes guiding questions in their own words, such as what evidence exists on phased versus simultaneous transitions, and runs each through the search tool and, separately, through library databases. Every reference the tool returns goes into a log with four checks: the item exists in a publisher or library record, the authors and date match, the finding the tool attributes to it appears in the text, and the study concerns papers of comparable size. Items that cannot be traced are recorded as such and excluded. The researcher compares the two result sets, noting what each route found that the other missed, and writes the scoping memo only from verified items.

acts.gate: The researcher writes the guiding questions, decides whether each returned reference exists, matches its authors and date, contains the attributed finding, and concerns comparable papers, and writes the scoping memo only from verified items.
acts.dl: A verified reference log and scoping memo for the researcher's own literature review, with untraceable items recorded and excluded.
acts.risk: Research-search tools vary in which paywalled journals they can read, so results may favor open-access and trade sources; the library database pass is the counterweight, and no student or participant data is involved.

acts.t: Does the Generated Melody Obey the Name and Meter?
acts.sum: Students in a music fundamentals or aural skills course each compose a short melody from a name, as in an openly licensed composition worksheet: the syllables fix the number of notes, each syllable receives a rhythmic value and a pitch, and every measure has to add up to the time signature. At college level the constraint set is extended with a stated key and a cadence on the final syllable. Each student then gives a music generation model the same constraints in words, using an invented name, and receives a short audio clip. The student transcribes the clip by ear into notation and checks it against the constraint list: whether the number of notes matches the syllable count, whether each measure contains the right number of beats, and whether the key and cadence were observed. Students perform both melodies and compare them. A brief written note identifies which constraints the model kept, which it ignored, and which of the student's own choices, such as placing the stressed syllable on a strong beat, came from knowing how the name is spoken.
acts.f: Computational Poetics and Procedural Generation
acts.gate: Each student composes a melody from a name under the stated constraints, transcribes the generated clip by ear, checks it against the constraint list, and notes which of their own choices came from knowing how the name is spoken.
acts.dl: A notated name melody, a transcription of the generated melody, and a constraint checklist comparing the two.
acts.risk: Music generation tools commonly limit free clips and require accounts, so a single class account may be used; transcription by ear calls for an alternative, such as working from a provided notation export, for students who are deaf or hard of hearing.

acts.t: Testing Chatbot-Suggested Interventions in a Forum Theatre Replay
acts.sum: A class devises and performs a short scene in which one character is treated unjustly, working in the Forum Theatre tradition that a published strategy page describes; the page may be read by link and is not reproduced. Between the first performance and the replay, small groups describe their own scene to a conversational assistant in a few sentences and ask what the mistreated character could try. Each group writes three of the suggestions on cards. During the replay, a spectator who stops the action draws a card and steps in to attempt that intervention against performers who stay in role and resist. An observer logs what happens: whether the suggested line could be said at all in the moment, how the antagonist responded, and what the spectator's body, voice and position in the space did that the card did not mention. Spectators then try interventions of their own. The debrief sorts the suggestions into those that held, those that collapsed against a resisting person, and those that assumed the antagonist would simply agree.

acts.risk: Scenes of mistreatment can touch students' own experience, so participation as spectator, observer or performer is a choice in this design; the chatbot step needs one device per group and a free tool.

acts.t: Auditing a Generated Neoclassical Image Before Drawing
acts.sum: Studio students choose a present-day moral principle or social issue and, before drawing, brief an image generator to render it in a Neoclassical style. Each student then audits the generated image against the design elements the class has identified by looking at Neoclassical paintings and sculpture: which features of the style the image reproduces, such as shallow stage-like space, sculptural figures and restrained gesture, and which it replaces with a generic antique look. The audit is written as a short list of observed features with the place in the image where each appears or is missing. Students go on to make a preliminary and then a final drawing or sculpture study of their own, deciding which conventions to keep and which the generated image handled poorly. Finished works are displayed in a crit in which classmates write their reading of each piece, with the visual clues that support it, before the maker states the intended message. The generated image and its audit hang beside the final work, so the group can see what came from the tool and what came from the maker.

acts.t: Sorting AI Stories About a Painting by Evidence
acts.sum: Students receive three short AI-written stories about one painting, prepared in advance by the instructor, together with a high-resolution open-access image of the work. The instructor produces the stories by prompting a conversational model with only the painting's title and artist, choosing a public-domain narrative painting whose image the holding museum has released for open use. Before reading the stories, each student records what they can see in the picture: figures, gestures, setting, light, objects. Working in pairs, students mark every narrative detail in the three stories as visible in the work, plausibly inferred from something visible, or not supported by anything in the picture, and note the passage of the image that settles each call. Pairs compare their markings and discuss cases where they disagree about what counts as inference. Each student then writes a short narrative from the point of view of one figure in the painting, footnoting the visual evidence for each claim about what that figure sees or does. A museum's published school program on telling stories from paintings is offered by link as a companion for faculty planning a gallery visit.

acts.t: Rehearsing a Restitution Case Against a Chatbot
acts.sum: In a unit on looting, restitution and repatriation, students prepare for a lawyers' role-play on the Parthenon sculptures by first arguing their assigned side against a conversational assistant. Each legal team instructs the assistant to take the opposing position, whether for retention in London or for return to Athens, and to rebut the team's points over several rounds. The team saves the transcript and sorts every argument the assistant made into those resting on a checkable fact, those resting on a legal or ethical principle, and those it cannot trace. Checkable facts, such as dates of removal, the terms of the permission claimed, or the content of museum and government statements, are looked up in the course readings and in the institutions' own published statements. Arguments that survive checking are carried into the live role-play, which runs without the assistant; arguments resting on untraceable claims are listed and dropped. After the role-play, the short comparison essay on a current heritage case asks students to name one argument from the rehearsal that changed their own position or sharpened it.

acts.gate: Students sort every argument the assistant made by its basis, check its factual claims against course readings and institutional statements, argue the live role-play without it, and name one argument that changed or sharpened their own position.
acts.dl: An annotated rehearsal transcript sorting the assistant's arguments by basis, a live role-play performance, and a short comparison essay.
acts.risk: A free conversational tool is sufficient, though account creation may be required; teams can share one account, and the lesson's license (CC BY-NC) limits reuse of its text to non-commercial settings with attribution.

acts.t: Querying a Grounded Assistant on Art and Authority
acts.sum: For a midterm review in an art history survey, students question a document-grounded assistant about how five ancient works express political authority, then check every passage it cites. The assistant holds only material the instructor has loaded: openly licensed survey readings and public-domain translations such as the prologue and epilogue of Hammurabi's laws and the Res Gestae of Augustus. Before class, students rank civic issues that matter to them, and each takes one, such as access to justice, as the lens for the review. A student asks the assistant how a work such as the Stele of Hammurabi, Seated Khafre or the Augustus of Primaporta relates to that issue, opens each cited passage, and records whether the passage says what the answer attributes to it and whether the answer describes anything visible on the object. Because the collection contains texts and no images, claims about form, scale, material or pose are tested by looking at the object in the museum's online record. Students then write a comparison of two cultures' systems of power that keeps only verified statements and adds their own formal observations.

acts.dl: A citation check log for the assistant's answers and a written comparison of two works using only verified claims plus the student's own formal observations.

acts.t: Occupation Prompt Audit of an Image Generator
acts.sum: Students generate images of people in ten occupations using one fixed prompt template, tally who is depicted, and then test which prompt revisions change the pattern. The class agrees on the template and the occupations, for example nurse, engineer, chief executive, cleaner and kindergarten teacher, and on a small coding sheet for apparent gender presentation, age, skin tone and setting, with an 'unclear' option. Each group produces the same number of images per occupation and enters its counts in a shared table. Coders compare a sample of each other's calls and discuss disagreements, since the categories are judgments about depictions and not facts about people. In a second round, groups revise the prompts in stated ways, such as adding a country, a decade or an explicit instruction about variety, and record which revisions shift the tallies and which leave them largely as they were. Results are set beside published labor statistics for the same occupations. Each group keeps a process log of prompts, counts and decisions, and closes by selecting one image it would be willing to use in a publication and explaining the choice.

acts.t: Committee Media Rights Register with Search Assistant
acts.sum: A program committee reviewing the media in its shared course materials uses a search-enabled assistant to locate openly licensed replacements, and confirms every reported license at the source page before anything is adopted. Members first inventory the images, audio and video clips in the shared slides and course shells and sort each item by the rights decision it calls for: copyrighted with permission on file, public domain, Creative Commons licensed, used under a fair use rationale, or generated or edited with AI. For items with no clear basis, a member describes the content needed and asks the assistant for openly licensed alternatives with the license it believes applies. The division of work is stated in the committee's procedure: the assistant searches and proposes; a named member opens each result, reads the license shown on the source page, and records whether it matches what the assistant reported. Mismatches and dead links are logged alongside confirmed items. The register that results gives, for each media item, its source, license, credit line and the date and name of the person who checked it.

acts.t: Tracing an Assistant's Links to Original Reporting
acts.sum: Students ask a search-enabled assistant what happened in a current news event and then follow every link it cites to find out where the information was first reported. The instructor names two or three events from the past week. Each pair saves the assistant's answer and its list of sources, opens each link, and classifies what it finds: original reporting by a news organization with named reporters or documents, a wire story republished elsewhere, aggregation or commentary about someone else's reporting, a press release or official statement, or a page that does not contain the claim attributed to it. Where a link leads to commentary, the pair keeps going until it reaches the reporting the commentary depends on, and notes how many steps that took. Pairs then send the identical question to a second system and compare which original reporting each one surfaced and which it passed over. The class tallies the categories on a shared board. A news literacy organization's lesson on telling news from content about news is offered by link as a companion for faculty who want a full lesson on that distinction.

acts.t: What a Research Agent Cannot Report
acts.sum: Reporting students delegate a bounded public-records question to an agentic research tool, audit each step it took, and then list what an investigative team would have had to do that the run could not. The question is set by the instructor from openly available local records, for example what a city's published inspection reports show about one category of business. Each group saves the agent's plan, the pages it visited and its final report, and checks every figure and attribution in the report against the page it came from. Steps are labeled as retrieval of an existing document, summary, calculation, or inference without a source. Alongside this, the class works through a published case use-case idea on watchdog journalism, used as published by link, as its example of an investigation carried out on the ground. Groups then write a two-column account: what the agent established from documents already online, and what reporters do that leaves no document for a tool to find, such as locating people, gaining their trust, observing a site, and confirming identities. A closing memo proposes the reporting plan needed to turn the findings into a story.
acts.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
acts.gate: Students check every figure and attribution against its source page, label each step the agent took, and write what reporters must do that leaves no document for a tool to find, closing with the reporting plan the story needs.
acts.dl: An annotated audit of the agent's run and a reporting-plan memo distinguishing document-based findings from reporting that requires presence and sources.
acts.risk: Agentic or deep-research modes are often limited to paid tiers, so an instructor-run session shared with the class may be needed; the question is confined to public records so no personal or confidential data enters the tool.

acts.t: Role-Playing a Reply to a Shared False Claim
acts.sum: Students practice responding to a friend or relative who has shared a false claim by rehearsing the conversation with a conversational assistant that plays that person. Each student writes a brief of their own: who the person is, how they know each other, what was shared, and how attached the person is to it. The claims are chosen by the class from already debunked examples listed by fact-checking organizations, so the factual question is settled before the conversation begins. The assistant is instructed to stay in character, to respond as that person plausibly would, and not to concede at once. After six to eight turns the student stops, saves the transcript, and marks the moments where the exchange opened up or closed down: a question that invited the other person to explain, a correction that landed as an accusation, a point of shared concern that was acknowledged or missed. Partners exchange transcripts and then replay one exchange face to face, each taking a turn as the person who shared the claim. A news literacy organization's slide use-case idea and infographic on speaking up are offered by link as published companions.

acts.t: Testing a Chatbot's Predictions About Chord Order
acts.sum: Beginning music students ask a conversational assistant to predict how reordering four common chords will change the feel of a loop, and then test each prediction by ear. The chords are the tonic, dominant, submediant and subdominant of a major key, the set behind a very widely used pop progression. Before consulting the assistant, each student writes their own guess about three reorderings: where the loop will feel most at rest, where it will pull forward, and whether it will sound brighter or darker. The assistant is then asked the same questions and its answers are saved. Students then listen to each ordering, either in a music software company's interactive browser lesson on this progression, used as published by link, or on a keyboard or guitar, and note what they hear, in their own words and with terms from class such as tension, release and cadence. The three accounts, the student's guess, the assistant's prediction and the listening notes, are set side by side. Discussion turns on where the verbal account matched the ear and where it was too general to test.

acts.gate: Students guess first about three chord reorderings, listen to each ordering and describe it in class terms such as tension and release, and judge where the assistant's predictions matched what they heard or were too general to test.

acts.risk: A free conversational tool and any instrument or free browser chord player are sufficient; students who are deaf or hard of hearing may need a visual or tactile representation of the progression.

acts.t: Trying an AI Staging Proposal on Its Feet
acts.sum: Acting and dramatic literature students receive a written staging proposal for one soliloquy from Hamlet, produced by a conversational model, and try it on their feet to find out which directions the language supports. The instructor generates the proposal in advance from the public-domain text of the speech, asking for blocking, pauses, gesture and the point of each move, and prints it without revision. Groups first read the speech aloud and mark its turns of thought, verse breaks and changes of address. They then stage the speech as the proposal directs and stop wherever a direction pulls against the text: a cross placed in the middle of a thought, a pause that breaks a verse line with no cue in the punctuation, a gesture toward someone the speech never addresses. For each direction, the group records kept, changed or cut, and quotes the line that decided it. Groups show their revised staging to one another and compare decisions. A theater company's teacher pack on the play, which approaches interpretive questions through physical rehearsal-room exercises, is offered by link as a companion for the session's wider practical work.

acts.t: Asking a Vision Model to Read Freeze Frames
acts.sum: Students studying Macbeth build freeze frames of chosen moments, photograph them, and ask a vision-capable model what emotion and relationship it reads in each still. Groups select a moment from the public-domain text and write down beforehand what they intend the image to show: who holds power, who is afraid, who is looking away. The photographs are the groups' own. The model is asked only to describe posture, gaze, distance and likely feeling, with no mention of the play. Its reading is set beside the group's stated intent and beside readings written by classmates who view the frame in the room. Where the model misses the intent, the group decides whether the physical choice was unclear, in which case they adjust level, spacing or focus and photograph again, or whether the model's reading reflects a narrow default about how emotion looks, in which case they keep the choice and say why. A short closing note quotes the lines each final frame carries. A theater company's program for deaf students, built on visually led work with the play, is offered by link as a companion.

acts.t: Tracing Chatbot Claims with a Citation-Showing Search Tool
acts.sum: Students work from a short chatbot answer on a topic from the course and test its factual claims one at a time with an AI search tool that shows its citations. The instructor generates the answer beforehand and hands it out with the prompt that produced it. Pairs split the answer into discrete claims, enter each into the search tool, and look for independent sources that bear on it, opening every cited page instead of relying on the tool's summary. A shared log records, for each claim, the sources found, whether they are independent of one another, and whether each citation the search tool offered supports what the tool said it did. The log therefore carries two layers of checking: the chatbot's claims against outside sources, and the search tool's citations against the pages they point to. The class closes by sorting the unsupported claims by type, such as a detail invented by the model, an outdated figure, or a one-sided framing. Day of AI's verification lesson is the idea-level starting point; none of its materials are used or entered into a tool.

acts.dl: A claim-by-claim verification log showing the sources located for each claim and whether each of the search tool's citations supports the statement attached to it.
acts.risk: Several AI search tools have free tiers, and the use-case idea can run from one projected instructor account if students lack accounts; queries contain only claims from the instructor-supplied answer, so no personal or student-authored text is entered.

acts.t: Committee Fact-Finding for a Student-Drafted AI Policy
acts.sum: In a multi-week unit, student committees draft clauses of an AI-use policy for their own course or program, and the campus-licensed AI assistant serves as both a subject of the policy and a witness to be questioned. Each committee asks the institutional assistant about itself: what it retains from a conversation, who can see that record, whether inputs are used for training, which features are switched on locally. The answers are treated as testimony, not as fact. Committee members then read the institution's published AI guidance, its privacy policy, and the vendor terms the institution links to, and mark each of the tool's statements as confirmed, contradicted, or not addressed in writing. Clauses are drafted only from the confirmed column, and the committee's report lists the open questions it referred to the campus IT or privacy office. Committees present their clauses to the full class for amendment and a vote. The idea of students moving an AI policy through a mock legislature comes from Day of AI's Student Senate unit, which is not reproduced here; the only text the tool receives is students' questions.
acts.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
acts.gate: Each committee produces a table marking the assistant's statements about itself as confirmed, contradicted, or not addressed in writing, policy clauses drafted only from the confirmed column, and the questions it referred to campus offices.
acts.dl: A committee report containing drafted policy clauses, a table of the assistant's statements about itself marked confirmed, contradicted, or unaddressed, and a list of questions referred to campus offices.
acts.risk: The design relies on a campus-provided assistant reached through institutional sign-on, so students need no personal account or payment; where no such tool exists, the fact-finding step has no direct substitute.

acts.t: Checking a Scripted Setback Overlay Against Hand Map Analysis
acts.sum: Groups in an introductory earth science course carry out Karl Wirth's landfill-siting investigation by hand and then compare their result with a GIS overlay script written by a coding assistant. In the published problem, groups read maps of surface water, land use, bedrock and surficial geology, and depth to bedrock against state siting regulations, consult well logs for promising areas, and rank three candidate sites. Here, after the hand analysis is complete, each group describes the setback rules in plain language to a coding assistant and asks for a script that applies them to public county data layers and maps the excluded zones. The script's output is laid over the group's hand-drawn exclusions. Every difference is traced to its cause: a regulation the group misread, a buffer distance the script got wrong, a layer with a different projection or date, a rule the group never told the assistant about. The poster documents the division of work between people and tool, the discrepancies found, and which version the final ranking rests on and why. The script and the prompts that produced it are appended.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Groups rank the candidate sites from their own hand analysis, trace every difference from the scripted overlay to its cause, and state which version their final ranking rests on and why.
acts.dl: A poster ranking three candidate sites, with a discrepancy table reconciling the hand analysis and the scripted overlay and the script and prompts appended.
acts.risk: Free coding assistants and open-source GIS software suffice, though running a script may need lab machines or instructor support; the handouts are BY-NC-SA 3.0 and the Minnesota Geological Survey maps carry their own terms.
