acts.t: Comparing Hand-Drawn Trees with Tree-Inference Software Output
acts.sum: First-year biology students draw phylogenetic trees by hand from three successive kinds of evidence and then compare their final tree with one produced by tree-inference software. The sequence follows Scott Cooper's interactive lecture segment: groups receive data on habitat and feeding behavior, then skeletal structures, then DNA sequences for a set of mammals, and redraw the tree as each data set arrives. In this version the hand-drawn DNA tree is set aside before any software is opened. The same sequences, or equivalents retrieved from a public sequence database, are then run through an alignment and tree-building tool, which in current packages may rely on statistical or machine-learned models of sequence change. The tool returns a finished tree with support values and no account of its reasoning. Groups mark each branch where the two trees differ and write the explanation the software does not give: which sites drive the difference, whether the alignment or the model accounts for it, and whether the support value warrants confidence. A selection of comparisons is projected and discussed.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: Groups produce hand-drawn trees from three successive kinds of evidence before any software is opened, and write the explanation the software does not give for each branch where the two trees differ.
acts.dl: A half-sheet pairing the group's hand-drawn DNA tree with the software's tree, with a written explanation for each branch that differs.
acts.risk: Free web-based alignment and tree-building services need no account, and a single projected run can serve a large lecture; the item is BY-NC-SA 4.0 and its downloadable files may carry their own reuse notes.

acts.t: Quotation Audit with a Source-Bound Assistant for a History Essay
acts.sum: Students writing a short argument essay on whether Reconstruction was a revolution, and for whom, use a document-grounded assistant limited to the assigned primary sources as a finding aid, and audit everything it returns before any of it reaches a footnote. The assignment follows the closed-corpus design of Caley Horan's first essay for an MIT survey of United States history since 1865: one historiographical prompt, answered from a fixed set of course sources with at least three primary sources cited. The instructor loads a set of public-domain Reconstruction-era documents, such as congressional testimony, Freedmen's Bureau records, and the amendments, into the assistant. Students ask it where the sources speak to their developing claim, and it answers with quotations and locations. Each returned quotation is checked word for word against the document, read in its surrounding paragraph, and logged as accurate, altered, misattributed, or not found in the source. Only verified passages enter the essay, cited in Chicago style. The audit log is submitted with the draft, and the argument, selection, and interpretation remain the student's.

acts.gate: The student makes the argument, selects and interprets the evidence, and submits an audit log marking every returned quotation accurate, altered, misattributed or not found in the source.
acts.dl: An argument essay of about 1,250 words with Chicago-style footnotes, submitted with a quotation audit log for every passage the assistant returned.
acts.risk: Only public-domain primary sources are loaded, since the readings attached to the original course need a separate rights check; an instructor-configured or institutional assistant spares students personal accounts, and the documents remain readable without the tool.

acts.t: Handing a Computational Protocol to an Agent to Find Gaps
acts.sum: A researcher who has written up the protocol for a computational step in their own study, such as a preprocessing pipeline or a statistical analysis, gives that protocol to an AI agent and watches where it cannot proceed. The design reworks the practical use-case idea in Rebecca Saxe's Week 3 assignment for a graduate course on robust science, in which a methods section is checked against reporting guidelines and a protocol is written and its snags recorded. Here the agent receives only the written protocol and a synthetic or public sample data set, in a sandboxed environment, and is asked to carry out the steps exactly as written and to report every assumption it makes. Each stall, guess, or silent default is logged: an unstated software version, a parameter the author knew by habit, a file-naming convention never written down. The researcher sorts the log into gaps in the protocol and errors of the agent, revises the protocol, and repeats the run. The revised protocol is then checked against the reporting guideline for the field, and the run logs are kept with the project record.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: The researcher decides which stalls and guesses are gaps in their own protocol and which are errors of the agent, and revises the protocol until it meets the field's reporting guideline.
acts.dl: A revised computational protocol with a gap log from each agent run, sorted into omissions in the protocol and errors made by the agent.
acts.risk: Agentic tools that execute code are often paid and need a sandbox; only synthetic or public data are supplied, so unpublished results and participant data stay out of the tool.

acts.t: Rendering a Program Logic Model and Auditing the Picture
acts.sum: A program committee preparing for a review writes its program's logic model as a plain-text specification, has an AI diagramming tool render it, and audits the picture against the text. The work follows the build-and-test procedure in the Community Tool Box section on logic models by Bobby Milstein and Tom Chapel: the committee draws the logic out of existing program documents, listing purpose, context, inputs, actions, outputs, and effects, and writes each link as an if-then statement. The specification goes to a diagram-generating tool, which returns a drawn model. Members compare the two line by line and record every arrow, box, or outcome the tool added, merged, renamed, or dropped. Additions are not discarded on sight: each is accepted, amended, or rejected with a stated reason, since a plausible but unrequested arrow may expose a link the committee had assumed without writing down. The corrected model then goes through the section's forward and reverse logic checks, and each link is labeled by the kind of evaluation question, need, process, outcome, or cost, that would test it. The specification contains program-level information only.
acts.f: Faculty and Staff Development
acts.gate: The committee decides whether each arrow, box or outcome the tool added, merged, renamed or dropped is accepted, amended or rejected, and records the reason for each decision.
acts.dl: A corrected logic model diagram with its text specification and a change log recording each element the tool added, merged, renamed, or dropped and the committee's decision on it.
acts.risk: The specification holds program-level information only, with no student records or personnel details; image output from such tools is often not screen-reader accessible, so the text specification is kept as the accessible version of record.

acts.t: Field Notes Versus a Vision Model on Street Photographs
acts.sum: Public health students conduct a walking survey of a neighborhood and then compare their own field notes with a vision-capable model's coding of the photographs they took. The fieldwork follows the Community Tool Box section on windshield and walking surveys by Phil Rabinowitz: teams of two or three settle guiding questions, build a checklist matched to them, and record housing condition, sidewalks, public spaces, businesses, signage languages, street life, and transit in notes and photographs. The walk itself is done without AI. Afterward, each team removes faces and license plates from a set of its photographs and asks a multimodal model to code them against the same checklist. The model's codes are set beside the team's notes for the same block. Teams list what the model reported that they missed, what it asserted that the image does not show, and what only presence on the street supplied: sound, smell, who greeted them, what the corner was like at five o'clock. The synthesis of assets, challenges, and differences between neighborhoods rests on the field notes, with the comparison reported as a methods appendix.
acts.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
acts.gate: Teams produce the field notes from a walk done without AI, the synthesis of assets, challenges and neighborhood differences, and a record of what only presence on the street supplied.
acts.dl: A community observation report synthesizing assets, challenges, and neighborhood differences, with a methods appendix comparing the model's photograph codes to the team's field notes.
acts.risk: The walk requires travel and may raise mobility and safety considerations, so a windshield or transit-based route is an alternative; faces, plates, and house numbers are removed before upload, and photographing residents may call for local review.

acts.t: How a Chatbot Summarizes a Biased 1903 Article
acts.sum: Learners in a research methods course read passages from a 1903 magazine article on left-handedness, identify the assumptions it carries, and then examine what a chatbot does with those assumptions when asked to summarize the same passages. The reading follows Magdalena Grose-Hodge's FORRT lesson on implicit bias and normative science, which starts with a historical text where bias is easy to see before turning to current research writing. After marking the article's claims about gender, race, mental health, and criminality by hand, learners paste the public-domain passages into a conversational assistant and request a plain-language summary. They set the summary beside their own annotations and classify each sentence: the framing is repeated, softened, corrected, flagged, or replaced by a new norm of the model's own. The questions asked of the output are whose voice is carried forward, whose is missing, and what the tool treats as the neutral position. A second prompt asks for a neutral rewrite of one sentence, which is checked against the original for whether the historical claim is still reported accurately. Contemporary abstracts are then read on paper, without the tool.

acts.t: Auditing an AI-Drafted Disclosure Against a Process Log
acts.sum: Students check whether an AI-drafted account of a fictional student's AI use is complete, using that student's process log as the record. The instructor writes the log: a dated sequence of the fictional student's prompts, pasted outputs, source lookups and draft revisions for a short essay in the course's subject. A document-grounded assistant, run by the instructor, receives only that log and is asked for a short disclosure statement on the fictional student's behalf. Working in pairs with printed copies, students trace each sentence of the drafted statement to log entries and list the uses the log shows that the statement omits, softens, or describes more generously than the entries warrant. Each pair then completes York University's AI-Based Tools: Declaration of Use form by hand for the fictional student, using the form as published and without entering it into any tool, and compares its completed form with the assistant's statement and with the instructor's actual course policy. Discussion turns on which omissions would matter under that policy and on what a log needs to contain for a disclosure to be checkable.

acts.t: Tracing an AI Answer's Claims Through Search-Backed Verification
acts.sum: Students take two factual claims from a saved AI answer on a course topic and follow them through a search-enabled assistant to the sources it cites, recording whether each cited page supports the claim. The instructor supplies the saved answer, generated beforehand without web access, so that every student starts from the same text. Each student asks the search-enabled assistant to verify the two chosen claims and then opens every link it returns. In a verification log the student records, for each link, whether the page exists, whether it says what the assistant reports, and whether it is a primary source, a secondary summary, or another machine-written text. The claims are then checked in a library database or the course text, which serves as the reference, and the student notes how relevant each source was to the question asked. With the log complete, students fill in York University's AI Use: Review and Reflection form as published, drawing the specific instances it asks for from their own log entries. The form itself is not entered into any tool.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: Students produce a verification log judging every link the assistant returned for existence, support, and source type, a check of each claim against a library database or the course text, and a reflection drawn from their own entries.
acts.dl: A verification log for two claims, listing every cited source with a support judgment, submitted with the completed reflection form.

acts.t: Testing AI Counterfactuals on the Fort Sumter Crisis
acts.sum: After completing Richard Latner's Crisis at Fort Sumter simulation as published, students ask a conversational assistant what would have followed had Lincoln taken a course he did not take, and then test each predicted consequence against the documentary record. The prompt is the student's own: a few sentences naming the alternative, for example evacuating the fort in March 1861, and asking for five consequences with reasons. Nothing from the simulation's pages, adviser texts or commentary is pasted into the tool. Students mark each consequence as supported, unsupported, or anachronistic, citing public-domain evidence: Lincoln's First Inaugural Address, cabinet members' written opinions on provisioning the fort, and correspondence printed in the Official Records. Where the assistant attributes a view to a named figure, students look for that view in the figure's own writing. In the class debrief, groups compare which kinds of claims the assistant handled with support, such as dates, offices and sequence, and which it asserted without evidence, such as motives and public reaction. Each student closes with a paragraph accepting, amending, or rejecting the counterfactual and giving grounds.

acts.gate: The student marks each predicted consequence supported, unsupported or anachronistic with a cited primary document, and writes a closing paragraph accepting, amending or rejecting the counterfactual with grounds.
acts.dl: An annotated table of the assistant's predicted consequences, each marked supported, unsupported or anachronistic with a primary-source citation, and a closing paragraph of judgment.

acts.t: Auditing an AI-Built Epidemic Curve
acts.sum: Students have a code-capable assistant build an epidemic curve and attack-rate table from an instructor-written outbreak dataset, then audit the result against the raw records. The use-case idea follows a session with Outbreak at Watersedge, the public health discovery game, played as published to introduce the sequence of an outbreak investigation; none of the game's case files or other content enters the tool. The instructor's dataset is a fictional foodborne outbreak of about sixty records with onset dates, symptoms, exposures and a few deliberate irregularities: missing onset dates, mixed date formats, and two records that fall outside the stated case definition. The assistant is asked for code that cleans the file, applies the case definition, plots cases by onset date, and computes attack rates by exposure. Students run the code and then recount cases by hand from the line list. They compare the two tallies, find how the code handled each irregular record, and check the attack rates against a two-by-two table built by hand. In the debrief, each group reports which of the code's unannounced choices changed the shape of the curve.

acts.gate: Students recount cases by hand from the line list, build a two-by-two table to check the attack rates, and list how the code handled each irregular record and which choices changed the curve.
acts.dl: An audit memo comparing the generated curve and attack rates with hand counts, listing each data-handling choice the code made and its effect.
acts.risk: The dataset is fictional and instructor-written, so no health data or student work enters a tool; the code can be run in a free browser notebook, and the game is listed as free of cost.

acts.t: Clustering Faculty Concerns About AI After Stinky Fish
acts.sum: At the start of a faculty workshop on AI in teaching, participants complete the Stinky Fish exercise as published on its method page, each writing a concern about AI in their courses that they have been carrying and sharing it briefly with the group. Afterward, with participants' agreement, a facilitator types the written concerns without names into an institutionally hosted assistant, which is asked to group them into themes and name each theme. The method page itself is not entered into the tool. The proposed clusters are projected, and participants check them against the original cards on the wall: each person finds their own card, says whether the theme label fits what they meant, and moves it where it does not. The group records which concerns the assistant merged that their authors consider distinct, and which concerns, held by only one or two people, disappeared into a larger theme. A second pass sorts the corrected themes by whether they concern personal know-how with the tools, the meeting of personal and professional use, or use in teaching itself. The corrected map sets the agenda for the remaining sessions.

acts.t: Second-Coding Panic Language in Historical Newspaper Pages
acts.sum: Students code the language and imagery of public-domain newspaper pages for moral panic features and then compare their coding with that of a multimodal AI model given the same page images. The class first works through the UK Data Service teaching resource on folk devils and moral panics as published, reading the archived materials from Stan Cohen's Mods and Rockers research on the Service's own site; none of those materials is uploaded to any tool. For the coding exercise the instructor selects scanned pages from a public-domain newspaper archive covering an earlier scare, such as 1890s reports on reckless bicycle riders. Each student notes an immediate reaction to a page, then codes it with an instructor-written codebook: who is named as the threat, exaggeration and prediction, calls for control, and how illustrations frame the group. The model receives the same images and codebook. Students tabulate agreement code by code, reread the page wherever they and the model differ, and decide which coding the page supports. A short memo separates what the student felt on first reading from what the text and images on the page show.

acts.gate: Each student produces an immediate reaction and a coding of each page, decides which coding the page supports wherever student and model differ, and writes a memo separating what they felt on first reading from what the page shows.

acts.t: Critiquing AI-Drafted Consent Wording Before Data Deposit
acts.sum: A researcher planning to archive interview data has a conversational assistant draft the data-sharing statements for a consent form and then critiques each draft the way the UK Data Service exercise Assessing consent form statements critiques its nine examples. The researcher begins without the tool, working through the exercise and its answers (Scott, UK Data Archive, 2026) to fix a personal standard for what ambiguous wording, unclear terms, and assurances that cannot realistically be kept look like. The assistant is then given a plain description of the planned study, written by the researcher, and asked for statements on anonymization, reuse, audio recordings, publication, destruction and archiving. For each one the researcher asks the exercise's questions: what this wording would mean for sharing the data, what is problematic or missing, and what wording would be clearer. Statements that promise more than the project can deliver, such as complete anonymity for audio, are rewritten to say plainly what steps will be taken. The revised form is checked clause by clause against the chosen repository's deposit and access conditions and the ethics board's required language.

acts.t: Voice Rehearsal for Raising a Data Integrity Concern
acts.sum: Graduate students rehearse aloud, with a voice-mode AI assistant playing a senior researcher, the conversation in which a trainee raises a concern about data in a document the senior researcher wrote. The assistant's brief is written by the instructor and uses an original scenario, for example a postdoctoral fellow who finds that a figure in a draft manuscript does not match the lab's shared spreadsheet; the brief has the character offer a plausible explanation and resist requests to see the underlying files. Students work in threes: one speaks with the assistant, one observes with a prepared sheet, one keeps time. The observer notes each point where the speaker accepts an explanation without asking for the data and each point where the speaker names a specific next step. Roles rotate. The group then performs the ORI casebook role play In a Stew over Cooked Data between human partners, using its role materials as published and entering none of them into the tool. The debrief compares the two conversations and checks the steps students proposed against the institution's research misconduct procedure.

acts.t: Checking an AI Review of a Specific Aims Draft
acts.sum: Graduate students write a one-page specific aims draft for a fictional project in their own field and submit it to a document-grounded assistant that holds the current NIH application instructions, then check every requirement the assistant cites against those instructions. Beforehand, the class reads a funded R21 application posted by the National Cancer Institute, Rebekka Lee's Effective Training Models for Implementing Health-Promoting Practices Afterschool, as a finished example; it is read on the posting page, unchanged, and no part of it is entered into the tool. The assistant is asked to comment on the draft's aims and to give, for each comment, the instruction it relies on and its reasoning. Students mark each comment as grounded in the instructions, as a reviewing convention the instructions do not state, or as unsupported. They then return to the sample and observe how a funded application handled the same point, such as the pairing of an aim with a hypothesis. Revision follows, with a short note on which comments were adopted, which were declined, and why.
acts.f: AI in the Writing Process: Invention, Feedback and Revision
acts.gate: Students write their own aims page, mark each comment as grounded in the instructions, a reviewing convention, or unsupported, and revise with a note on which comments they adopted, which they declined, and why.
acts.dl: A revised specific aims page for a fictional project, with an annotated list of the assistant's comments marked grounded, conventional or unsupported.
acts.risk: Drafts describe fictional projects, so no unpublished research ideas enter a tool; the NCI sample is restricted to unchanged, credited, nonprofit educational use and is read at its posting page.

acts.t: Auditing an Agentic Folder Reorganization With a Checklist
acts.sum: A researcher lets an agentic AI tool reorganize a working copy of a project folder and then audits what it did using the research data management checklist from The Turing Way. The copy is made first and the original set to read-only, following the checklist's item on leaving raw data untouched with a backup; sensitive or consent-restricted files are left out of the copy. The tool is asked to propose and apply a folder structure and naming convention, write a README, and keep a log of every action. The researcher then works down the checklist's individual list and its research-team list, credited there to Borghi and van Gulick (2022): could every group member find and use the materials, are naming conventions and folder structures in place, is documentation kept with the data, could an outside researcher use what is there. A file-by-file comparison of the copy with the original, using checksums, shows whether any data file was altered and which changes the tool made without logging them. Changes that pass the audit are applied to the real project by hand.
acts.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
acts.gate: The researcher decides which of the tool's changes pass the checklist and the checksum comparison, identifies any it made without logging, and applies only the approved changes to the real project by hand.
acts.dl: A scored checklist for the reorganized copy, a list of unlogged or data-altering changes, and a set of changes approved for the real project.
acts.risk: Agentic tools often require a paid plan and broad file permissions; the audit runs on a copy that excludes sensitive or consent-restricted data, and nothing is changed in the original.

acts.t: Reviewing AI-Written Code With a Review Checklist
acts.sum: Students act as code reviewers for a small analysis function and test suite written by a code assistant, using the file-level questions in The Turing Way's Checklist for code review process. Each student specifies a function from the course's current material, for instance one that computes a rolling mean over a time series with missing values, and has the assistant produce the function and its unit tests. The student opens a pull request containing the generated code and reviews it as the checklist's reviewer role describes: whether inputs are checked, loops terminate, interfaces and types are clear, and the unit tests test what they claim. Students write additional tests for edge cases the generated tests skip, such as empty input or a window longer than the series, and run both sets. Program-level items are applied as well, including whether the licenses of all imported libraries are documented and compatible. The review ends with a written decision to approve, request changes, or reject, with each finding tied to a checklist item and a test result. Reviews are then presented to a small group, which questions the reviewer's decision.
acts.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
acts.gate: The student writes the specification, adds tests for edge cases the generated tests skip, and decides to approve, request changes or reject, tying each finding to a checklist item and a test result, then defends it before a small group.
acts.dl: A written code review on a pull request, with added tests, findings keyed to checklist items, and an approve, request-changes or reject decision.
acts.risk: A free code assistant and a free repository host are sufficient, though both typically need an account; students' specifications, not graded work, are what enter the assistant.
